title: What is light? The fastest messenger in the universe

summary.text: This unit is about what light is and how fast it goes. Light is energy that travels, even through empty space where there is no air. It is the fastest thing there is: about 3 lakh kilometres every second. Even so, sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us, so we always see the Sun as it was a little while ago. Light acts like a wave, and it also comes in tiny packets called photons. Every star we see is a message that light has carried across space, and scientists still argue about what light really is deep down.
summary.art: A beam of sunlight shooting from the Sun to a child's face in an Indian courtyard, with a small clock floating beside the beam showing 8 minutes, and the beam drawn half as a wavy line and half as a row of tiny dots.

intro.hook: Go into a dark room with a torch. Switch it on. Did the light take any time to reach the far wall? Or was it there at once?
intro.text: It looks instant. Click, and the wall is bright. For thousands of years, most people thought light needed no time at all to travel. Then, about 350 years ago, a young astronomer noticed that one of Jupiter's moons seemed to run late. Sometimes it was late by many minutes. The moon was not late at all. The light carrying its picture was. In this unit, you will find out how fast light really is, why the sunshine on your arm is about 8 minutes old, and why light is stranger than anyone guessed.
intro.art: A child in a dark room pointing a torch at a far wall, a question mark hanging in the beam between the torch and the bright circle.

outcomes: I can say what light is: energy that travels in straight lines and needs no air to move through.
I can say how fast light goes, and explain why the sunlight I see left the Sun about 8 minutes ago.
I can run a fair test to show that light reaches me before sound, and use the gap to work out how far away lightning is.
I can tell how people found out light is not instant: Galileo's lanterns, Rømer's late moon and Fizeau's spinning wheel.
I can explain that light acts like a wave and also comes in tiny packets called photons.
I can explain why looking far away is looking back in time, and say what a light-year is.
I can say what scientists agree about light, and what nobody knows yet.

terms.meaning: Light is energy that travels. It lets us see. It also warms things up.
terms.example: Sunlight warms your arm on a winter morning.
terms.art: Sunbeams falling through a window onto a warm cat.

terms.meaning: Energy is what makes things happen. It can move things, warm things or light them up.
terms.example: A lit diya gives out light energy and heat energy.
terms.art: A diya flame with arrows of light and heat spreading out.

terms.meaning: A light source is a thing that makes its own light.
terms.example: The Sun, a candle, a torch and a firefly are light sources. The Moon is not. It shines with sunlight.
terms.art: A row of the Sun, a candle, a torch and a firefly, each glowing.

terms.meaning: Speed is how far something goes in a certain time.
terms.example: A cycle might go 15 kilometres in an hour. Light goes about 3 lakh kilometres in one second.
terms.art: A cycle, a train, a rocket and a beam of light in a race, the beam far ahead.

terms.meaning: The speed of light is how fast light travels in empty space. It is about 3 lakh kilometres every second.
terms.example: In one second, light could go round the Earth about seven and a half times.
terms.art: A beam of light looping round the Earth seven and a half times.

terms.meaning: A vacuum is a space with nothing in it, not even air.
terms.example: Space between the Sun and the Earth is almost a vacuum. Light crosses it easily. Sound cannot.
terms.art: An empty jar with a sign 'no air inside', and a beam of light passing through.

terms.meaning: A ray is a thin line of light going in one direction.
terms.example: A ray of sunlight through a gap in the curtains looks like a straight bright line in dusty air.
terms.art: A straight bright line of sunlight crossing a dusty room.

terms.meaning: A wave is a wiggle that travels. The water does not travel with it. The wiggle does.
terms.example: Drop a stone in a pond. Rings of ripples spread out, but the water mostly bobs up and down.
terms.art: Rings of ripples spreading in a pond, a leaf bobbing in one place.

terms.meaning: The wavelength is the distance from one top of a wave to the next top.
terms.example: Ripples in a bucket might be 2 centimetres apart. Light's waves are far, far smaller, thinner than a hair.
terms.art: A wavy line with a ruler between two tops.

terms.meaning: A photon is one tiny packet of light. Light is made of a huge number of them.
terms.example: A torch sends out more photons in one second than there are grains of sand on a beach.
terms.art: A torch beam drawn as a stream of millions of tiny glowing dots.

terms.meaning: An electromagnetic wave is a wiggle in electricity and magnetism that travels through space. Light is one kind.
terms.example: Radio waves, microwaves and X-rays are cousins of light. They are the same kind of wave, with different wavelengths.
terms.art: A long ladder of waves, from long radio waves to short X-rays, with a small rainbow band in the middle marked 'light we can see'.

terms.meaning: An electron is a tiny part of every atom. It carries electric charge.
terms.example: When an electron in an atom drops down to a lower energy, it gives out a photon.
terms.art: An atom with an electron jumping down and a tiny glowing dot flying off.

terms.meaning: A light-year is how far light travels in one year. It is a distance, not a time.
terms.example: One light-year is about 9 lakh crore kilometres. The nearest star after the Sun is about 4 light-years away.
terms.art: A beam of light running past a calendar with 365 days, a measuring tape behind it.

terms.meaning: An astronomer is a scientist who studies the Moon, planets, stars and galaxies.
terms.example: Ole Rømer was an astronomer who timed one of Jupiter's moons in 1676.
terms.art: A person at a telescope at night, writing in a notebook.

terms.meaning: Jupiter is the biggest planet. It has many moons. Io is one of them.
terms.example: Io goes round Jupiter in about 42 and a half hours, and hides behind it every time.
terms.art: Jupiter with a small moon beside it, half in the planet's shadow.

terms.meaning: A messenger is something that carries news from one place to another.
terms.example: A postman is a messenger. Light is a messenger too. It carries pictures of the stars to us.
terms.art: A postman on a cycle and a beam of starlight, both carrying a little letter.

terms.meaning: Lightning is a giant spark in the sky. Thunder is the sound it makes.
terms.example: You see the flash first and hear the thunder later, because light is much faster than sound.
terms.art: A lightning bolt over a village, and a child counting on their fingers.

terms.meaning: A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same.
terms.example: To compare light and sound, we make the flash and the bang at the very same moment.
terms.art: Two identical setups side by side with only one thing different.

terms.meaning: Gravity is the pull between all things that have mass. It keeps us on the ground.
terms.example: Very heavy things, like the Sun, can even bend the path of light a tiny bit.
terms.art: A beam of starlight curving slightly as it passes the Sun.

terms.meaning: A galaxy is a huge family of stars, gas and dust, held together by gravity.
terms.example: We live in the Milky Way galaxy. Its light-band crosses the sky on very dark nights.
terms.art: A spiral galaxy seen from far away, with a tiny arrow pointing to 'you are here'.

explanations.definition: Light is energy that travels outwards from a light source, in straight lines, even through empty space.
explanations.description: Light is a kind of energy. It comes out of light sources like the Sun, fire and bulbs. It shoots away from them in straight lines, in every direction. When it lands on something, it can warm it, or bounce into our eyes so we see. Light does not need air or water to travel through. It crosses empty space easily. That is how sunlight reaches us across 15 crore kilometres of nearly empty space.
examples: Sunlight warms a steel tumbler left on the windowsill.
A torch beam goes straight. It does not curl around a door.
On the Moon there is no air, but sunlight still lights it up.
explanations.art: A Sun in the middle of the page with straight rays shooting out in all directions, some landing on a planet, a plant and a tumbler.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what light is.

explanations.definition: In empty space, light travels 299,792,458 metres every second. We round this to about 3 lakh kilometres per second.
explanations.description: Light is the fastest thing in the universe. In empty space it goes about 3 lakh kilometres every second. That is so fast that it could go round the whole Earth about seven and a half times in one second. A cricket ball from a fast bowler goes about 40 metres in one second. A jet plane goes about 250 metres. Light goes 30 crore metres. To us it looks instant, but it is not. It just needs very little time for short trips.
examples: Light crosses your room in far less than a blink. A blink takes about one tenth of a second.
Light from the Moon takes about 1 and a third seconds to reach you.
Radio signals, which travel at the speed of light, took about 1 and a third seconds to reach Earth from Chandrayaan-3 near the Moon.
explanations.art: A race track with a snail, a cyclist, a cricket ball, a jet plane and a beam of light, the beam already looping round a tiny Earth.
explanations.context: Light seems to arrive instantly. This card is about how fast it really goes.

explanations.definition: Light takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel from the Sun to the Earth.
explanations.description: The Sun is about 15 crore kilometres away from us. Even at light's speed, that trip takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds. So when sunlight touches your face, it left the Sun about 8 minutes ago. If the Sun suddenly went dark, we would not know for 8 minutes. The sky would stay bright until the last light arrived. (This can never really happen. The Sun has fuel for billions of years.) The same is true of everything you see. You always see things as they were, a tiny moment ago.
examples: The sunrise you watch left the Sun about 8 minutes before you saw it.
Your friend across the room is seen about one hundred-millionth of a second in the past.
A radio message to Mars takes between about 3 and 22 minutes, depending on where the two planets are.
explanations.art: A beam of light leaving the Sun with a clock showing 12:00, arriving at a child on Earth with a clock showing 12:08.
explanations.context: Light is very fast, but space is very big. This card is about why the sunlight you see left the Sun a few minutes ago.

explanations.concept: Light needs no air, sound does
explanations.definition: Light can travel through empty space. Sound needs something like air, water or a wall to travel through.
explanations.description: Sound is a wiggle passed from one bit of air to the next. With no air, there is nothing to pass it on. So space is silent. Light is different. It does not need anything to travel through. It is a wiggle in electricity and magnetism itself. In air, light is also almost a million times faster than sound. Sound goes about 1 kilometre in 3 seconds. Light goes 3 lakh kilometres in 1 second. That is why you see lightning before you hear thunder.
examples: You see a firecracker burst in the sky before you hear the bang.
At a big cricket ground, you see the bat hit the ball a moment before you hear the 'tock'.
Astronauts outside a spacecraft cannot hear each other without radios. Radios use light-like waves.
explanations.art: Two panels: in one, sound waves pushing air bits along like a crowd. In the other, a beam of light crossing a starry, empty space.
explanations.context: Light and sound both carry news to us. This card is about how they are different.

explanations.definition: The number of seconds between a lightning flash and its thunder, divided by 3, gives the distance in kilometres.
explanations.description: Lightning makes its flash and its thunder at the same moment. The flash reaches you almost at once. The thunder walks behind it, about 1 kilometre every 3 seconds. So count the seconds from the flash to the thunder. Then divide by 3. That is about how many kilometres away the lightning was. If the gap is getting shorter, the storm is coming closer. If you can hear thunder at all, the storm is close enough to be dangerous. Go indoors.
examples: A 6-second gap means the lightning was about 2 kilometres away.
A 15-second gap means about 5 kilometres away.
A crash with no gap means the lightning was very close.
explanations.art: A child at a window counting on fingers between a flash and a 'BOOM', a map showing the storm 2 kilometres away.
explanations.context: During a storm, you see the flash before you hear the thunder. This card shows how to use that gap.

explanations.concept: How people found out light is not instant
explanations.description: For a very long time, people argued about whether light takes any time at all. It is so fast that no ordinary test could tell. Here are the main steps in the argument, in order. Today the question is settled. Light has a speed, and we know it exactly.
examples: In 1638 Galileo suggested two people with lanterns on far-apart hills. He could not see any delay.
In 1676 Ole Rømer saw Jupiter's moon Io seem late when the Earth was further from Jupiter.
In 1849 Hippolyte Fizeau measured it on Earth, with a spinning toothed wheel and a mirror about 8 kilometres away.

perspectives.who: Many thinkers of the old world, including the Greek thinker Aristotle and later the French thinker René Descartes
perspectives.explanation: Light is instant. It needs no time at all. Descartes said that if light took time, we would see eclipses of the Moon happen at the wrong moment.

perspectives.who: Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist, in his book Two New Sciences, 1638
perspectives.explanation: Light might be very fast but not instant. He suggested a test with two lanterns on far hills. When it was tried, nobody could see a delay. He could only say light was very fast.

perspectives.who: Ole Rømer, a Danish astronomer working in Paris, 1676
perspectives.explanation: Light takes time. Jupiter's moon Io seemed to hide behind Jupiter later when the Earth was further away. The extra time was the time light took to cross the extra distance. Christiaan Huygens used his numbers to work out a speed close to the real one.
Rømer was right. Light has a speed. Since 1983, the metre itself has been defined using the speed of light. So the speed of light in empty space is now an exact, agreed number.

explanations.art: A timeline: Galileo with a lantern on a hill, Rømer at a telescope pointed at Jupiter, Fizeau with a spinning toothed wheel.
explanations.context: Light's speed was argued about for centuries. This card tells how people found out the answer.

explanations.definition: Nothing that carries energy or a message can travel faster than light travels in empty space.
explanations.description: In 1905 Albert Einstein, a young clerk in a patent office in Switzerland, put forward a new idea. He said the speed of light is the same for everyone, however fast they are moving. Every test since has agreed. From this, he showed that nothing can carry a message faster than light. Light is the speed limit of the universe. Our fastest spacecraft, the Parker Solar Probe, goes about 190 kilometres every second. That is very fast, but light is more than 1,500 times faster.
examples: If you ran beside a light beam at half its speed, it would still race away from you at full speed.
No rocket can ever catch up with a light beam.
When a star explodes far away, its light is the first news that can reach us. Nothing can arrive sooner.
explanations.art: A rocket straining to chase a beam of light, the beam far ahead with a sign 'speed limit 3 lakh km per second'.
explanations.context: Light is very fast. This card is about why scientists think nothing can ever be faster.

explanations.definition: Light travels fastest in empty space. It travels more slowly through things like water, glass and air.
explanations.description: The speed of light, 3 lakh kilometres a second, is its speed in empty space. When light goes into water or glass, it slows down. In water it goes about three quarters as fast. In glass about two thirds as fast. When it comes out into air again, it speeds up again. In 1999, a Danish scientist named Lene Hau shone light through a cloud of atoms cooled to almost the coldest cold there is. The light slowed to about 17 metres a second. A car on a city road goes about that fast. Two years later, her team stopped light completely for a moment, then let it go again.
examples: In a glass of water, light goes about 2 lakh 25 thousand kilometres a second.
In a diamond, light goes less than half its speed in space.
In Lene Hau's super-cold cloud, a cyclist going downhill could beat light.
explanations.art: Three lanes: light racing in space, a little slower in water, slower in glass, and a cyclist overtaking a glowing beam inside a frosty cloud.
explanations.context: Light is fastest in empty space. This card is about how it slows down inside things like water and glass.

explanations.description: For over 300 years, scientists argued about what light is made of. Is it a stream of tiny bits, like sand thrown from a hand? Or is it a wave, like ripples on a pond? Each side had good evidence. The surprising answer is that light behaves like both. Here are the main views, in order.
examples: Ripples in two places on a pond cross and make a pattern. Light does that too, which is wave-like.
A glow-in-the-dark star lights up under blue light but not under red light. That shows light's energy comes in packets.
A phone camera's sensor counts light as tiny hits, one packet at a time.

perspectives.who: Isaac Newton, an English scientist, in his book Opticks, 1704
perspectives.explanation: Light is a stream of tiny bits, which he called corpuscles. That is why it goes in straight lines and makes sharp shadows.

perspectives.who: Christiaan Huygens, a Dutch scientist, in his Treatise on Light, 1690, and Thomas Young, an English doctor, around 1803
perspectives.explanation: Light is a wave. Young shone light through two thin slits close together. On the wall behind, he saw bright and dark stripes. Only waves make stripes like that, where two sets of ripples add up or cancel out.

perspectives.who: James Clerk Maxwell, a Scottish scientist, in 1865
perspectives.explanation: Light is a wave of electricity and magnetism. His sums gave the speed of such a wave. It came out the same as the speed of light.

Light also comes in tiny packets of energy. Later these were named photons. This explained why dim blue light can knock electrons out of a metal, but bright red light cannot. He won the Nobel Prize for this.

Light is neither an ordinary wave nor an ordinary particle. It is a quantum thing. It travels like a wave and arrives as packets. The sums of quantum physics predict how it behaves extremely well. What it is really like, deep down, is still argued about.

explanations.art: A split picture: on one side ripples spreading on a pond, on the other side tiny glowing dots flying like thrown sand, a beam of light in the middle wearing both.
explanations.context: Scientists argued for 300 years about whether light is a wave or a stream of tiny bits. This card tells the story.

explanations.definition: A photon is a single packet of light energy. Light is made of photons.
explanations.description: A photon is the smallest possible bit of light. You cannot have half a photon. A torch sends out an enormous number every second. That is why light looks smooth, the way a heap of sugar looks smooth from far away. Each photon carries a little energy. A blue photon carries more energy than a red one. That is why blue or purple light can make a glow-in-the-dark star shine, but red light cannot, however bright it is. Each red photon is too weak to do the job alone.
examples: Very dim light from a far galaxy reaches a telescope camera one photon at a time.
Solar panels work because photons knock electrons loose inside them.
Too much ultraviolet light, which has strong photons, can burn your skin. Red light cannot.
explanations.art: A heap of sugar that looks smooth, and a magnifying glass showing it is made of grains, next to a torch beam magnified into separate glowing dots.
explanations.context: Light looks smooth, like flowing water. This card is about how it is really made of tiny packets.

explanations.definition: Light is given out when electrons in atoms drop from a higher energy to a lower energy.
explanations.description: Every atom has tiny electrons around it. When an atom gets extra energy, from heat or electricity, its electrons jump up to a higher energy. When they drop back down, they give out that energy as a photon. That is where light comes from. A hot coal glows because its atoms are shaking and their electrons keep giving out photons. In the Sun's centre, atoms crash together and make huge amounts of energy. That energy slowly works its way out and leaves the Sun's surface as sunlight.
examples: A tube light makes light when electricity gives energy to a gas inside it.
A hot iron rod in a blacksmith's shop glows red, then orange, then yellow as it gets hotter.
A firework's colours come from different atoms giving out photons with different energies.
explanations.art: An atom with an electron dropping from an outer ring to an inner ring, a tiny glowing photon flying out, and a blacksmith's glowing rod in the background.
explanations.context: Light has to start somewhere. This card is about where it comes from, deep inside atoms.

explanations.concept: The long journey out of the Sun
explanations.description: Sunlight takes 8 minutes to reach us from the Sun's surface. But its energy was made deep in the Sun's centre. The Sun's insides are so crowded that a photon only goes a tiny way before it is swallowed by an atom and given out again in a random direction. So the energy wanders, bumping its way out, for a very long time. Scientists work this out with sums, because nobody can look inside the Sun. Their estimates range from about ten thousand to over one hundred thousand years.
examples: The warmth on your face may have been made inside the Sun before people in India first grew wheat and barley.
Imagine trying to leave a packed railway platform at Diwali. You keep being pushed back. Energy leaving the Sun is a bit like that.
Once it reaches the surface, the last part of the trip, to Earth, takes just 8 minutes.

perspectives.explanation: Different ways of doing the sums give different answers, from about ten thousand to over one hundred thousand years. They agree it is a very long time.

explanations.art: A cut-open Sun with a zigzag path wandering from the centre to the surface, labelled 'thousands of years', and a straight line from the surface to Earth labelled '8 minutes'.
explanations.context: Sunlight takes 8 minutes to reach us. This card is about the much longer trip the energy took inside the Sun first.

explanations.concept: Light is the messenger of the cosmos
explanations.definition: Light from far away tells us about distant places, as they were when the light left them.
explanations.description: We cannot travel to the stars. Almost everything we know about them was carried to us by light. Light tells us where a star is, how hot it is and even what it is made of. But light takes time, so looking far away is looking back in time. A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9 lakh crore kilometres. A star 100 light-years away is seen as it was 100 years ago. The oldest light of all, a faint glow left over from the young universe, set out about 13.8 billion years ago.
examples: The Moon you see is about 1 second old.
Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is seen as it was about 8 and a half years ago.
The Andromeda galaxy, a faint smudge on very dark nights, is seen as it was about 25 lakh years ago, before modern humans existed.
explanations.art: A child looking up at the night sky, with labels on the Moon '1 second ago', a star '8 years ago' and a faint galaxy '25 lakh years ago'.
explanations.context: We cannot visit the stars. This card is about how light brings us news of them, and why that news is always old.

explanations.definition: Light passing close to something very heavy, like the Sun or a galaxy, follows a curved path. This is called gravitational lensing.
explanations.description: Einstein said that very heavy things bend space around them. Then light passing close by follows a curved path. In 1919, during a total eclipse of the Sun, two teams of astronomers photographed stars near the darkened Sun. One team went to an island off Africa, led by Arthur Eddington. The other went to Brazil. The stars seemed a tiny bit out of place, about as much as Einstein had said. Today astronomers use this bending like a giant magnifying glass in space. The Indian-born astronomer Priyamvada Natarajan uses it to map dark matter, which we cannot see.
examples: A whole galaxy can bend the light of a galaxy behind it into an arc or a ring.
This is called gravitational lensing.
It is different from light bending in water or glass. Here it is space itself that is curved.
explanations.art: A heavy galaxy in the middle of space, with light from a far galaxy behind it curving around it into a glowing ring.
explanations.context: Light goes in straight lines. This card is about how very heavy things in space can bend its path.

explanations.description: We can predict what light will do extremely well. But what a photon is between leaving a lamp and landing on a detector is still argued about. Labs can send light one photon at a time through two slits. Each photon lands as one dot. After thousands of dots, wave stripes appear. If a detector checks which slit each photon went through, the stripes disappear. Here, 'detector' means any measuring machine. It does not need a person or a mind to watch.
examples: One photon at a time makes one dot at a time.
Thousands of dots slowly build up a striped wave pattern.
Checking which slit the photon used makes the stripes go away.

perspectives.who: Niels Bohr, a Danish scientist, and his followers
perspectives.explanation: Before it is measured, a photon has no exact path. We should only talk about what the measuring machines record.

perspectives.who: Louis de Broglie and later David Bohm
perspectives.explanation: Tiny particles really do take one path each. A hidden wave guides them, and that wave goes through both slits. How well this works for light is still argued about.

perspectives.who: Hugh Everett, an American scientist, in 1957
perspectives.explanation: Every possible result really happens, each in its own branch of reality.
The sums work perfectly, and we may never know which picture is true. Some say we should just use the sums. The question is still open.

explanations.art: A screen slowly filling with single dots that gradually form bright and dark stripes, with a small detector box beside one slit.
explanations.context: Light behaves like both a wave and packets. This card is about the puzzle of what it really is.

agreed.text: Light travels at about 3 lakh kilometres every second in empty space, and nothing can carry a message faster.
agreed.evidence: It has been measured in many different ways, from Rømer's moon in 1676 to lasers bounced off mirrors that astronauts left on the Moon in 1969.

agreed.text: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach the Earth.
agreed.evidence: We know the Sun's distance and the speed of light. Radio signals from spacecraft near the Sun arrive with exactly the delays these numbers predict.

agreed.text: Light can travel through empty space, but sound cannot.
agreed.evidence: Sunlight and starlight reach us across nearly empty space. Inside a jar with the air pumped out, a ringing bell can be seen but not heard.

agreed.text: Light behaves like a wave and also comes in packets called photons.
agreed.evidence: Light through two slits makes wave stripes. But sensitive cameras record that same light arriving as single dots, one photon at a time.

agreed.text: Looking far away in space means looking back in time.
agreed.evidence: When a star explodes in another galaxy, we see the explosion years after it happened. The further the galaxy, the older the news.

agreed.text: Very heavy things bend the path of light.
agreed.evidence: Stars near the Sun looked shifted during the 1919 eclipse, and today we photograph many galaxies bent into arcs and rings.

challenging.claim: Light is instant. It needs no time to travel.
challenging.who: Many thinkers for about 2,000 years, including Aristotle and René Descartes. It is also what our eyes tell us every day.
challenging.for: When you switch on a lamp, the room lights up at once. No ordinary test shows any delay.
challenging.against: Rømer's late moon in 1676, and Fizeau's spinning wheel in 1849, both showed light takes time. Today we measure the delay to the Moon and back, about 2 and a half seconds.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that light takes no time at all, and why scientists gave it up.

challenging.claim: Our eyes send out rays that touch the things we look at.
challenging.who: Some Greek thinkers, such as Euclid and Ptolemy.
challenging.for: It feels as if we reach out with our eyes. We say someone 'casts a glance'.
challenging.against: In about 1021, Ibn al-Haytham, a scientist in Cairo, argued that light comes into the eye from things. Your eye sees a star at once when you open it, though the star is far away. Rays from the eye would take time to get there.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of how light and eyes work. A whole other unit is about how we see.

challenging.claim: Light is a wave that needs something to travel through, a hidden jelly filling all of space called the 'ether'.
challenging.for: Every other wave they knew, like sound and water waves, needs something to wiggle. So light should too.
challenging.against: In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley looked for the Earth rushing through the ether. They found nothing. Einstein's ideas in 1905 explained why no ether is needed.
challenging.context: This card is about the 'ether', a substance scientists once thought filled space, and why they gave up the idea.

challenging.claim: Light is just a wave, nothing more.
challenging.who: Most scientists between about 1870 and 1905, after Young and Maxwell.
challenging.for: Light makes stripes after passing through two slits, which only waves do. Maxwell's sums described light as a wave perfectly.
challenging.against: Einstein showed in 1905 that light's energy comes in packets. Robert Millikan tested this carefully and found Einstein was right, though Millikan had hoped to prove him wrong.
challenging.context: Scientists once thought light was only a wave. This card is about why they changed their minds.

challenging.claim: A single photon can be seen by a human eye.
challenging.who: A team led by Alipasha Vaziri in Vienna, in a 2016 paper.
challenging.for: In their tests, people reported seeing single photons a little more often than pure guessing would allow.
challenging.against: The effect was small, and only a few people were tested. Many scientists want more tests before they agree.
challenging.context: Photons are the tiny packets light comes in. This card is about whether a human eye can notice just one.

challenging.claim: Something might travel faster than light after all.
challenging.who: Some people, after a 2011 experiment called OPERA seemed to find tiny particles called neutrinos going faster than light.
challenging.for: The first results really did seem to show it, and the scientists shared them openly, asking others to check.
challenging.against: The team then found a loose cable in their timing equipment. With it fixed, the neutrinos were not faster than light. Every other test agrees with Einstein.
challenging.context: Scientists think nothing can travel faster than light. This card is about a time it seemed something did, and what really happened.

big_questions.q: If every sight reaches you a little late, is there any moment you see exactly 'now'?
big_questions.hint: Light from your hand takes a tiny bit of time to reach your eye. Light from the Sun takes 8 minutes.

big_questions.q: Why can light cross empty space when sound cannot?
big_questions.hint: Sound needs air to be passed along. What is light a wiggle of?

big_questions.q: How can one thing be both a wave and a stream of tiny packets?
big_questions.hint: Maybe 'wave' and 'particle' are our words, borrowed from ripples and sand. Does light have to fit our words?

big_questions.q: Where does light go after it lands on something?
big_questions.hint: Touch a black car roof in the afternoon sun. What do you feel?

big_questions.q: If a star you are looking at had already stopped shining, how would you know?
big_questions.hint: Think about how long its light has been travelling.

big_questions.q: Why should there be a speed limit in the universe at all?
big_questions.hint: Nobody fully knows. Maybe space and time are made in a way that needs it.

big_questions.q: The light we see from the Sun gave life to plants, which fed us. Are we made of sunlight?
big_questions.hint: Follow your dinner back. Rice grew in a field. What did it need from the sky?

big_questions.q: If someone on a planet 100 light-years away looked at the Earth with a giant telescope today, what would they see?
big_questions.hint: The light they see left the Earth 100 years ago. What was happening in India then?

big_questions.q: Some news, like light from a far star, is very old when it reaches us. Is old news still true?
big_questions.hint: Think about letters, photographs and stories from grandparents.

big_questions.q: Scientists can predict what light does perfectly, but still argue about what it is. Can you understand something without knowing what it is?
big_questions.hint: Do you know what your best friend really is? You still know how they will laugh.

big_questions.q: Who gets remembered for a discovery? Rømer worked out light's delay, but his boss did not believe him.
big_questions.hint: Should we believe a new idea because of who says it, or because of the evidence?

story.title: The Moon That Was Never Late
story.note: Ole Rømer, Giovanni Cassini, the Paris Observatory, Jupiter's moon Io and Rømer's prediction that Io would appear about ten minutes late on 9 November 1676 are real. Cassini really did not accept Rømer's idea. Marthe, her father the clock-keeper, her brother Luc and his letters are made up.
text: In the autumn of 1676, in Paris, there was a girl called Marthe whose father kept the clocks. Not the clocks of a house, but the great clocks of the Royal Observatory, a tall white building on a hill outside the city. Every evening he wound them, oiled them and checked them against the stars. Marthe carried his lamp.

The clocks mattered because of Jupiter. Through the long telescopes, Jupiter was a bright little disc with four tiny moons beside it. The nearest moon was called Io. Every forty-two and a half hours, Io slipped into Jupiter's shadow and vanished. Then it came out again on the other side. It was as steady as a temple bell. The great astronomer Cassini had written tables saying when Io would vanish and appear, for months ahead. Sailors far out at sea could use those tables to find where they were.

Marthe's brother Luc was one of those sailors. He had left in the spring on a ship bound for the islands across the ocean. His letters came back with other ships, and Marthe kept them under her pillow.

There was a young astronomer at the observatory, a tall, quiet Dane called Ole Rømer. He was not famous. He spoke French with a funny accent, and he wrote down everything. On clear nights Marthe watched him crouch at the eyepiece, calling out, 'Now!' at the very moment Io appeared. Her father would read the clock, and Rømer would scratch the time in his book.
One cold night, Rømer frowned at his book for a long time.
'She is late again,' he said.
'Who is?' asked Marthe.
'Io. In the spring she came out early. Now, every month, she is a little later. Cassini's tables are good. The clocks are good. Your father's clocks are the best in France. And still she is late.'
'Maybe she is tired,' said Marthe. Rømer laughed, but he did not stop frowning.

That week a letter came from Luc. Marthe ran up the hill with it. 'He says the sea is calm and he is well,' she told her father. Then she stopped, and read the date at the top again. The letter was more than five weeks old. Luc had written it far out on the ocean, and it had crossed all that water slowly, on another ship, before it reached her. While she was reading 'the sea is calm', there might be a storm around him now. She would not know for weeks.
'His letters get older,' she said quietly. 'The first one, from the port at Le Havre, came in two days. This one took five weeks. The further he goes, the older the news is when it gets here.'
Rømer had been listening. He put down his pen.
'Say that again, Mademoiselle.'
'The further away he is, the older his news.'
Rømer went to the big drawing of the heavens pinned on the wall. He drew the Sun in the middle and the Earth's circle around it. Further out he drew Jupiter.

'In the spring,' he said, 'the Earth was here, on the side of its circle near Jupiter. Since then, the Earth has been travelling round the Sun, away from Jupiter. Now we are much further from it.' He tapped the drawing. 'What if Io is not late at all? What if she comes out of the shadow exactly on time, out there? But the news of it, the light carrying her picture, needs time to reach us. And the further we are, the longer it takes.'
'Like Luc's letters,' said Marthe.
'Like Luc's letters. Everyone says light arrives the moment it leaves. Descartes said so. Maybe they are all wrong. Maybe light is a messenger, and messengers need time.'

He spent the next weeks doing sums. One evening in September he stood before all the astronomers of the Academy of Sciences. He made a prediction. On the ninth of November, he said, Io would come out of Jupiter's shadow about ten minutes later than Cassini's tables said. Not because the moon was slow. Because the light was travelling.
Some of the gentlemen smiled into their sleeves. Cassini was polite, but he shook his head.

On the night of the ninth of November, the sky was clear and very cold. Marthe held the lamp low so it would not dazzle anyone. Her father stood at the clock. Rømer sat at the telescope, still as a heron.
The time in Cassini's tables came. The astronomers leaned forward. Jupiter shone, with its little moons. But where Io should have been, there was only dark.
A minute passed. Two. Five. Someone coughed. Marthe could hear the clock's slow tick, tick. Eight minutes. Nine.
'Now!' said Rømer.
A tiny spark of light stood beside Jupiter. Her father read the clock. It was about ten minutes after the time in the tables.
Nobody spoke for a while. Even Cassini said nothing.

Afterwards, walking down the hill, Marthe looked up. The sky was crowded with stars, sharp and white. She had always thought she was seeing them now. But if light needed minutes to come from Jupiter, it must need far longer from the stars. Some of the light falling into her eyes might have left before she was born. Perhaps before Paris was built. The whole sky was a bundle of letters, each one written long ago, all arriving tonight at once.
Many astronomers did not believe Rømer. Cassini never did. It took about fifty years before everyone agreed that light has a speed. But Marthe believed him that very night.

At home she took out Luc's letter and read it again. 'The sea is calm,' he had written. It was old news now. But it was still Luc's voice, still true for the moment he wrote it. She held it near the candle and read it slowly, the way you might look at a star.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Io was never late. Its eclipses happened on time, but the light carrying the news needed extra minutes to cross the extra distance when the Earth was further from Jupiter. Light is very fast, but it is not instant. So everything we see, especially in the sky, is a message from the past. Marthe's brother's letters, older the further he sailed, are the same idea at the speed of a ship. The story also quietly asks why a true idea from a young unknown man was doubted, and what it takes to believe evidence over a famous name.
ask: Rømer said Io was not late at all. Then why did it seem late?
How were Luc's letters like the light from Io?
The astronomers smiled into their sleeves. Why do you think some of them did not believe Rømer?
When Marthe looked at the stars walking home, what did she realise?
Is an old letter, or old starlight, still true? What do you think?

games.title: How Old Is This Light?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game. Each card shows something that gives out light, from a phone in your hand to a far galaxy. You line them up by how long their light took to reach you.

printables.title: 16 light cards to cut out
items: A phone screen in your hand
A street light at the end of the road
A lighthouse 20 kilometres out at sea
Lightning in a storm 5 kilometres away
Betelgeuse, the red star in Orion
The Orion Nebula, a glowing cloud in Orion's sword
The oldest light: the glow left over from the young universe

printables.title: 16 matching time cards
items: Less than a millionth of a second (phone)
Less than a millionth of a second (bulb)
About a millionth of a second (street light)
About one fifteen-thousandth of a second (lighthouse)
About one sixty-thousandth of a second (lightning)
About 1 hour 7 minutes to 1 hour 32 minutes (Saturn)
About 500 to 700 years, still being measured (Betelgeuse)

printables.title: A long strip: the Light-Age Line

rules: Cut out the 16 light cards and the 16 time cards. Keep the time cards in a separate pile, face down.
Lay the Light-Age Line on the floor. 'NOW' is on the left, the oldest light on the right.
On your turn, take a light card. Put it on the line where you think it belongs, from youngest light to oldest.
Say why you put it there. A good reason wins a star token, even if the place is wrong.
When all the light cards are down, turn over the time cards one by one and match each to its light card.
Move any card that was in the wrong place. Each card that was already right wins its player a star token.
The player with the most star tokens wins.

setup.art: A long paper strip on the floor, labelled NOW at the left end and BILLIONS OF YEARS at the right end.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the Light-Age Line on the floor.

setup.art: A child placing a card with a picture of the Moon near the left end of the strip, other cards fanned in their hand.
setup.caption: 2. Put each light card where you think it goes.

setup.art: A time card '8 minutes' being laid next to a Sun card, and a star token beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Turn over the time cards and check.

flow.do: 1. Lay the Light-Age Line on the floor. 2. Shuffle the 16 light cards. 3. Keep the time cards face down in a separate pile.
flow.say: Every card shows something that gives out light. Light takes time to travel. So the light from each thing is a little bit old when it reaches us. We are going to line them up, from the youngest light to the oldest.
flow.kid: Lay the long strip on the floor. NOW is on the left. Very old light is on the right. Mix up the light cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of How Old Is This Light?, a card game about how long light takes to reach us. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Play the Moon card and the Sun card together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise. Which light is older when it reaches us, the Moon's or the Sun's?
flow.kid: Practice round. Which light took longer to reach you, the Moon's or the Sun's? Tap your answer.

check.q: Which light took longer to reach your eye?
options: Both arrive at the same moment
check.why: The Sun is about 400 times further away than the Moon. Moonlight takes about 1 and a third seconds. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes. Picking the Moon often means thinking the Moon is further because it looks smaller at night. Picking 'the same moment' usually means thinking light is instant.

ask.q: Why is the Sun's light older?
good: The Sun is much further away.
Light needs more time for a longer trip.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player places one light card on the line. 2. They say why they put it there. 3. Give a star token for a good reason.
flow.say: When you put your card down, tell us why. Is it near or far? Is it on Earth, in the solar system, or out among the stars?
flow.kid: Take turns. Put your card on the line. Say why. A good reason wins a star!
flow.parent: Good reasons: things on Earth are nearest, so their light is youngest. Planets come next. Stars are much further, so their light is years old. Galaxies are further still. Planets move, so their times change. Mars and Venus can be near or far, depending on where they are in their orbits. That is why their cards show a range.

flow.do: Turn over the time cards one by one. Match each one to its light card. Move any light card that was in the wrong place.
flow.say: Now let's check. Some of these numbers will surprise you.
flow.kid: Turn over the time cards. Match each one. Were you right? Move any that were wrong.

check.q: Lightning is 5 kilometres away. How long does its light take to reach you?
check.why: Light from lightning reaches you in about one sixty-thousandth of a second. It is the thunder that takes about 15 seconds, because sound is far slower. Picking 15 seconds usually means mixing up the flash and the sound.

flow.think: If you could see a planet 13 light-years away, what would its light show about you? What were you doing 13 years ago?

games.title: Photon Tag
games.players: 3 or more players, outdoors or in a big hall
games.context: This is a running game based on the founder's idea of photon tag. Photons are the tiny packets light comes in. They travel in straight lines, so in this game you may only run in straight lines.

printables.title: 8 call cards for the caller
items: PHOTON: run in straight lines only
WAVE: link arms and move in a long wavy line
PARTICLE: break apart, each person is one dot
SUN: everyone starts from the middle and runs outwards
STAR: walk very slowly, your light has a long way to go
GLASS: slow down to two thirds of your speed
SPACE: full speed, nothing in your way

rules: One player is the caller. Everyone else is a photon.
Photons may only run in straight lines. To turn, you must stop, plant your feet, then set off in a new straight line.
The caller holds up a call card and shouts it. Everyone must do what it says.
If a photon curves while running, it is out for one round.
Swap the caller after every 4 cards.
