setup.caption: 1. All photons start at the Sun in the middle.

setup.art: Children running away from the centre in straight lines like the spokes of a wheel, one child stopped and turning.
setup.caption: 2. Run only in straight lines. Stop to turn.

setup.art: Children with linked arms making a wavy line across the ground.
setup.caption: 3. On WAVE, link arms and move like a wave.

flow.do: 1. Draw a circle, the Sun, in the middle of the play area. 2. Everyone stands inside it. 3. Choose a caller.
flow.say: Light leaves the Sun in straight lines, in every direction. You are all photons, tiny packets of light. When I say go, run out of the Sun in a straight line.
flow.kid: You are a photon! Stand in the Sun circle. When the caller says go, run out in a straight line.
flow.context: This is the first step of Photon Tag, a running game about light. Photons are the tiny packets light comes in. Here you set up the game.
flow.parent: Play somewhere safe and open. Watch that straight-line runners do not crash into each other.

flow.do: The caller holds up call cards one at a time. Everyone acts them out.
flow.say: Listen to the caller! Photon means straight lines. Wave means link arms and move together. Particle means break apart.
flow.kid: Listen to the caller. Do what each card says. Remember: no curving!

ask.q: Why do we have to stop to turn?
good: Light only changes direction when it hits something.

check.q: In the game, the GLASS card makes photons slow down. What does that show about real light?
check.why: Light goes about two thirds as fast inside glass as in empty space. When it comes out, it speeds up again. Picking 'stops' usually means thinking glass blocks light, but glass lets light through. Picking 'speeds up' mixes it up the wrong way round.

flow.do: Sit down together and talk about the game.
flow.say: Was light more like a wave or more like a crowd of particles in our game? Scientists found that real light is both at once.
flow.kid: Sit down. Was light a wave or a crowd of dots in the game? Real light is both!
flow.think: How can something be a wave and a crowd of dots at the same time?

items.p: What is light?
opts: A kind of energy that travels
Something that only comes from bulbs
items.why: Light is energy that travels out from light sources, like the Sun, fire and bulbs. Picking 'a kind of air' usually means mixing up light with the air it shines through. Light even crosses space, where there is no air.
items.art: A Sun sending straight rays outwards.

items.p: How fast does light travel in empty space?
opts: About as fast as a jet plane
It takes no time at all
items.why: Light goes about 3 lakh kilometres every second. Picking '1 kilometre every 3 seconds' mixes light up with sound. Picking 'no time at all' is the old idea that light is instant, which Rømer showed was wrong.

items.p: Sunlight takes about ____ minutes to reach the Earth.
items.why: The Sun is about 15 crore kilometres away. Even at light's speed, that takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds.

items.p: Light needs air to travel through.
items.why: False. Light crosses the empty space between the Sun and the Earth. Sound needs air, but light does not.

items.p: When you look at the Sun's light, you are seeing it as it was a few minutes ago.
items.why: True. The light took about 8 minutes to reach you. So you see the Sun as it was when that light left it. Never look straight at the Sun, though.

items.p: In a storm, why do you see the lightning before you hear the thunder?
opts: Light travels much faster than sound
Your eyes work faster than your ears
Sound is blocked by the rain
items.why: The flash and the thunder are made at the same moment. Light reaches you almost at once. Sound travels about 1 kilometre every 3 seconds. Picking 'thunder is made later' is a common idea, but they happen together. Picking 'eyes work faster' puts the gap in your body, not in the trip.

items.p: You see lightning. You count 9 seconds until the thunder. About how many kilometres away was the lightning?
items.why: Sound travels about 1 kilometre every 3 seconds. 9 divided by 3 is 3. So the lightning was about 3 kilometres away.

items.p: In the Flash and Bang experiment, a helper banged steel plates 200 big steps away. What did you notice?
opts: I saw the plates meet, then heard the bang
I heard the bang, then saw the plates meet
I saw and heard them at exactly the same time
items.why: Light and sound left the plates together. Light arrived almost at once. Sound took a moment longer. Picking 'heard first' means thinking sound is faster. Picking 'the same time' is true when you are very close, but not from 200 steps.

items.p: What is a photon?
items.why: Light is made of tiny packets of energy called photons. A torch gives out an enormous number of them every second. Picking 'camera' comes from the word 'photo', which also comes from the Greek word for light.

items.p: In the Glow Star Test, which light made the glow star shine?
items.why: Each blue photon carries enough energy to make the star glow. Each red photon does not, so even lots of red light does not work. Picking 'bright red' usually means thinking brightness is what matters.

items.p: Match each thing to how long its light takes to reach you.
items.why: The further away something is, the longer its light takes to reach us. The Moon is near, the Sun further, stars much further, galaxies further still.

items.p: Put these in order, from the one whose light is youngest when it reaches you, to the oldest.
items.why: Your hand is closest, so its light takes almost no time. The Moon is about 1 second away, the Sun about 8 minutes, and stars are years away.

items.p: Nothing can carry a message faster than light.
items.why: True. Einstein showed in 1905 that light is the speed limit of the universe. Every test since has agreed.

items.p: Draw the Sun, the Earth and a beam of light between them. Write how long the light takes on the beam.
items.a: A Sun, an Earth, a straight line between them, labelled about 8 minutes.
items.why: Light travels from the Sun in straight lines and takes about 8 minutes to reach us.
items.art: An empty space with a Sun on the left and a small Earth on the right.

items.p: Your friend says, 'Light is instant. It takes no time at all.' What would you tell them? Use one piece of evidence.
items.a: Light is very fast, but it does take time. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us from the Sun. Rømer found that Jupiter's moon Io seemed late when the Earth was further away, because its light had further to travel.
items.why: Light seems instant on Earth because the distances are short. Over the huge distances of space, its travel time shows.

items.p: Why is space silent, but full of light?
items.a: Sound needs air or something else to pass it along, and space has almost nothing in it. Light does not need anything to travel through, so it crosses empty space.
items.why: Light is a wiggle of electricity and magnetism, which can travel through empty space. Sound is a wiggle of air.

items.p: Ole Rømer saw Jupiter's moon Io seem late. What did he decide?
opts: The light carrying its picture needed more time when the Earth was further away
Jupiter was moving away from the Sun
items.why: Io was never late. The light had a longer trip when the Earth was further from Jupiter. Picking 'Io was slowing down' is what you might think first. Picking 'broken clocks' was checked, and the clocks were fine.

items.p: In 1638, Galileo tried to measure light with lanterns on two hills. Why didn't it work?
opts: Light was too fast for the people to time it
items.why: Light crosses a few kilometres in a tiny fraction of a second. People react in about a quarter of a second. So the test only measured people's reactions. Picking 'too dim' misses that brightness does not change light's speed.

items.p: Light goes into a glass of water. What happens to its speed?
opts: It slows down, to about three quarters of its speed in space
items.why: Light is fastest in empty space. In water it goes about three quarters as fast. When it comes out, it speeds up again. Picking 'it stops' usually means thinking water blocks light, but you can see through water.

items.p: Lene Hau, in 1999, slowed light down to about 17 metres a second. How did she do it?
opts: She shone it through a cloud of atoms cooled to almost the coldest cold possible
She used a very thick wall
She used a very dim torch
She made the light very red
items.why: In her super-cold cloud of atoms, light crawled at about the speed of a car in a city. Picking 'dim torch' mixes up brightness with speed. Dim light travels just as fast as bright light.

items.p: A ____ is how far light travels in one year.
items.why: A light-year is a distance, not a time. It is about 9 lakh crore kilometres.

items.p: The microwaves in the Chocolate experiment made melted spots 6 centimetres apart. Why do microwaves tell us about light?
opts: Microwaves are the same kind of wave as light, and travel at the same speed
Microwaves are slower than light, so they are easier to see
Microwaves are a kind of sound
items.why: Light, radio waves and microwaves are all electromagnetic waves. They travel at the same speed in empty space. Picking 'slower' is a common guess, but they are just as fast. Picking 'sound' mixes them up with sound waves, which need air.

items.p: In the Chocolate experiment, the melted spots were 6 centimetres apart. The spots are half a wave apart. How long is one whole wave, in centimetres?
items.why: The spots are half a wave apart. So a whole wave is 6 + 6 = 12 centimetres.

items.p: Thomas Young shone light through two thin slits. He saw bright and dark stripes. What did this show?
items.why: Only waves make stripes like this. Where two waves add up you get bright, and where they cancel you get dark. Like the ripples crossing in the thali. Picking 'instant' mixes up two different questions about light.

items.p: Einstein said light comes in packets. What are the packets called?
items.why: Photons are packets of light. Electrons are tiny parts of atoms that can give out or soak up photons. Picking 'rays' mixes up the path light takes with what it is made of.

items.p: Bright red light has stronger photons than dim blue light.
items.why: False. Bright red light has more photons, but each red photon is weaker than each blue photon. That is why it cannot make a glow star glow.

items.p: Light from a star 100 light-years away left that star about 100 years ago.
items.why: True. A light-year is how far light travels in one year. So light from 100 light-years away has been travelling for 100 years.

items.p: Sort these. Does it travel through empty space, or does it need something to travel through?
items.why: Light and its cousins, like radio waves, can cross empty space. Sounds need air, water or something solid to pass them along.

items.p: Where does light come from, deep inside atoms?
opts: Electrons dropping to a lower energy give out photons
Atoms are full of tiny bulbs
Light is stored in atoms like water in a tank
Atoms catch light from the air
items.why: When an electron gets extra energy, it jumps up. When it drops back down, it gives out a photon. Picking 'stored like water' misses that light is made fresh each time.

items.p: Rømer's boss, Cassini, did not believe him. Was it right to doubt him? What finally showed Rømer was right?
items.a: It is fair to doubt a new idea and ask for evidence. But Rømer's prediction came true: Io appeared about ten minutes late on 9 November 1676. Later measurements, like Fizeau's spinning wheel in 1849, agreed that light has a speed.
items.why: Good scientists doubt new ideas until there is evidence, then change their minds. Who says it matters less than what the evidence shows.

items.p: In the Glow Star Test, why can't lots of red light do what a little blue light can?
items.a: Light comes in packets called photons. Each blue photon has enough energy to make the glow star glow. Each red photon does not, and lots of weak packets cannot add up to do the job of one strong one.
items.why: This is the same idea that won Einstein his Nobel Prize: the photoelectric effect.

items.p: Light goes about 3 lakh kilometres every second. How far does it go in 2 seconds? Write your answer in lakh kilometres.
items.why: 3 lakh kilometres each second, for 2 seconds, is 3 + 3 = 6 lakh kilometres.

items.p: Sunlight takes 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach us. How many seconds is that?
items.why: 1 minute is 60 seconds. 8 minutes is 8 × 60 = 480 seconds. 480 + 20 = 500 seconds.

items.p: The Moon is about 1 and a third light-seconds away. Astronauts left mirrors on the Moon. A laser flash goes there and bounces back. About how long until it returns?
items.why: The light has to go there and come back, so it is twice the trip. 1 and a third plus 1 and a third is about 2 and a half seconds. Picking 1 and a third forgets the return trip. Picking 8 minutes mixes the Moon up with the Sun.

items.p: You are on Mars. You send a radio message home. Radio travels at the speed of light. It takes 12 minutes. When does your family hear you?
items.why: Radio waves are cousins of light and travel at the same speed. If Mars is 12 light-minutes away, the message arrives 12 minutes later. A reply takes another 12 minutes. That is why you cannot have a normal phone chat with Mars. Picking 'at the moment' means thinking radio is instant.

items.p: A star is 600 light-years away. Tonight, it explodes. When could people on Earth see the explosion?
items.why: The light from the explosion must travel 600 light-years to reach us. That takes 600 years. Picking 'tonight' means thinking light is instant over any distance. Picking '600 days' mixes up years and days.

items.p: Light from a galaxy 25 lakh light-years away shows us that galaxy as it was 25 lakh years ago. What does this mean for astronomers?
opts: Looking further away is like looking further back in time
The galaxy must be gone now
items.why: Light from far away is old news. So the further away a galaxy is, the further back in time we see it. Picking 'the galaxy must be gone' is a common worry, but most galaxies last billions of years. Picking 'fake' misses that old news is still true news about the past.

items.p: In 1919, astronomers photographed stars near the Sun during a total eclipse. The stars seemed slightly out of place. Why?
opts: The Sun's gravity bent the stars' light a tiny bit
The Moon's shadow moved the stars
items.why: Einstein said heavy things curve space, so light passing near the Sun bends. The measurements agreed with him. Picking 'the stars really moved' misses that the stars returned to their usual places when the Sun moved on.

items.p: Labs can send light through two slits one photon at a time. Each photon makes one dot on a screen. What appears after thousands of dots?
opts: Two plain stripes, one for each slit
items.why: Each photon lands as one dot, like a particle. But together the dots build up the stripes that only waves make. This is why scientists say light behaves like both. Picking 'two plain stripes' is what you would expect from tiny marbles, and it is not what happens.

items.p: In quantum physics, the 'observer' that changes the result must be a person watching.
items.why: False. In physics, 'observer' means anything that measures, such as a detector or a camera. No person or mind needs to watch. The stripes vanish whenever any detector records which slit the photon used.

items.p: Scientists agree completely on what a photon really is between leaving a lamp and landing on a detector.
items.why: False. The sums of quantum physics predict light's behaviour extremely well. But what a photon is really like on its journey is still argued about.

items.p: Match each person to what they found about light.
pairs: light takes time to travel, from Jupiter's moon Io
light makes wave stripes through two slits
light is a wave of electricity and magnetism
light comes in packets, later called photons
light slowed to about 17 metres a second
items.why: Each of them added one piece to what we know about light, over more than 300 years.

items.p: The fastest spacecraft goes about 190 kilometres each second. Light goes about 3 lakh kilometres each second. Light is about how many times faster? Choose: 15, 150 or 1,500.
items.why: 300,000 divided by 190 is about 1,579. The nearest choice is 1,500. Even our fastest spacecraft is very slow compared with light.

items.p: Why do astronomers call light 'the messenger of the cosmos'? Give two things light tells us about stars.
items.a: We cannot visit the stars, so almost everything we know about them comes from their light. Light tells us where a star is, how bright and hot it is, and even what it is made of. It also tells us how the star was in the past, when the light left it.
items.why: Cecilia Payne used starlight in 1925 to show that stars are mostly hydrogen. Meghnad Saha, from India, worked out in 1920 how a star's light shows how hot it is.

items.p: Light behaves like a wave and also comes in packets. Describe one piece of evidence for each.
items.a: Wave: light through two slits, or through fine cloth, makes a pattern of bright and dark spots, like crossing ripples. Packets: the glow star shines under dim blue light but not bright red, because each photon's energy matters. Cameras also record light as single dots.
items.why: Scientists say light is a quantum thing. It travels like a wave and arrives as packets.

items.p: If you could ride on a beam of light from the Sun, describe your trip to the Earth. How long would it take? What would you pass?
items.a: I would leave the Sun's surface and fly in a straight line. I would pass Mercury after about 3 minutes and Venus after about 6. After about 8 minutes and 20 seconds I would reach the Earth.
items.why: Einstein wondered about riding a light beam when he was 16. Thinking like this helped him find his ideas about space and time.

items.p: Draw light as a wave and as photons, in one picture. Label which part is which.
items.a: A wavy line from a lamp, with small dots along it, each labelled photon, and the wave labelled wave.
items.why: Light travels like a wave and arrives as photons. A drawing like this is a model, a picture that helps us think.
items.art: A lamp on the left and a wall on the right with empty space between.

experiments.title: Flash and Bang: does light beat sound?
experiments.context: In this experiment, a helper far away makes a flash and a bang at the same moment. You see when the flash arrives and hear when the bang arrives. Then you find out which is faster, light or sound.
experiments.question: When a flash and a bang happen at the same moment far away, which reaches me first, and does the gap grow when I am further away?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will you see the flash and hear the bang together? Or will one come first? Will the gap be bigger from 200 steps away than from 50 steps away?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, the helper makes the flash and the bang at exactly the same moment, every time. Only the distance changes. Do 3 tries at each distance, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: Was there a gap? Tiny, small or big?

materials.item: two steel plates or two steel lids to bang together
a helper, a grown-up or an older child
a long open space, like a playground, a cricket ground or an empty lane
a phone stopwatch, if you have one
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up must come. Choose a safe place away from traffic. Do not bang the plates near anyone's ears.

schedule.what: Go to an open place. Test the flash and bang from 20, 100 and 200 big steps away. Fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the helper far away, with an arrow for the light and an arrow for the sound. Draw the light arrow arriving first.

setup.art: A grown-up holding two steel plates high above their head at one end of a playground, a child standing close by.
setup.caption: 1. Stand close to the helper first. Watch and listen.

setup.art: The child far away at the other end of the playground, counting big steps, the helper small in the distance.
setup.caption: 2. Walk 100 big steps away, then 200.

setup.art: The helper banging the plates together high in the air, a line of light reaching the child's eyes and a slower curly line of sound still on its way.
setup.caption: 3. Watch the plates meet. Listen for the bang.

flow.do: 1. Stand right next to the helper. 2. The helper holds the plates high and bangs them together once. 3. Watch and listen.
flow.say: Close up, the flash of the plates meeting and the bang seem to happen together. Let's see if that changes when we move far away.
flow.kid: Stand close to the helper. Watch the plates bang. Did you see it and hear it at the same time?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Flash and Bang experiment. A helper bangs two steel plates, and you check whether you see it before you hear it.

ask.q: What do you guess will happen when you are far away?

flow.do: 1. Walk 100 big steps away from the helper and turn round. 2. Wave to show you are ready. 3. The helper bangs the plates 3 times, with a pause between. 4. Watch the plates closely each time. 5. Write down what came first.
flow.say: Watch the plates very closely. Notice the moment they meet. Now listen. Does the bang come at that moment, or a little after?
flow.kid: Walk 100 big steps away. Watch the plates meet. When do you hear the bang? Write it down.
flow.parent: At 100 big steps, about 70 metres, the bang arrives about one fifth of a second after you see the plates meet. It is small but most children notice it. If not, move further away.

flow.do: 1. Walk on to 200 big steps away, about 140 metres. 2. Repeat 3 bangs. 3. Write down the results. 4. If you have room, try 300 big steps too.
flow.say: Further away now. Is the gap bigger, smaller or the same?
flow.kid: Walk to 200 big steps. Watch again. Is the gap bigger now?

check.q: You moved twice as far from the helper. What happened to the gap between seeing and hearing?
check.why: Sound needs about twice as long to travel twice as far, so the gap grows. Light still arrives almost at once. Picking 'smaller' usually means thinking sound speeds up. Picking 'the same' usually means thinking the gap comes from the helper, not from the trip.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Come back together. Talk about why the flash arrived first.
flow.say: The light and the sound left the plates at the very same moment. The light reached you almost at once. The sound took longer. So which one is faster?
flow.kid: The light and the sound left together. The light won the race. Which is faster?

ask.q: How long did the light take to travel 200 steps?
good: Less than a millionth of a second.

ask.q: What else do you see before you hear?
good: A cricket bat hitting a ball far away.

flow.do: Explain how this works for thunderstorms.
flow.say: Lightning is the same. The flash and the thunder happen together. Light reaches us almost at once. Thunder travels about 1 kilometre every 3 seconds. So count the seconds and divide by 3 to find how far away the lightning is.
flow.kid: Lightning works the same way. Count the seconds from the flash to the thunder. Divide by 3. That is how many kilometres away it is.
flow.parent: Safety: if you can hear thunder at all, the storm is close enough to be dangerous. Count from indoors. Never shelter under a tree.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like scientists. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: light is much faster than sound. What I saw: from 200 steps, I saw the plates meet before I heard the bang every time. Why: the light and sound started together, but light travels so fast it arrived almost at once, while sound took a moment.

experiments.title: The Glow Star Test: light comes in packets
experiments.context: In this experiment, you shine red light and blue light on glow-in-the-dark stars. You find out which colour makes them glow. The answer shows that light comes in tiny packets called photons.
experiments.question: Will bright red light make a glow-in-the-dark star glow as well as dim blue light does?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess. Will a bright red light charge the glow star? Will a dim blue light charge it? Which one will make it glow more?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same kind of glow star each time. Shine each light for the same time, 20 seconds, from the same distance. Keep the room dark. Let the star go completely dark before each new test.
results_table: How strong was the glow? None, faint or bright

materials.item: glow-in-the-dark star stickers
a phone with a screen you can set to plain red, then plain blue
a torch
red and blue cellophane sheets, or clear plastic you colour with markers
a dark room or a cupboard

experiments.safety: Do not shine any light straight into anyone's eyes. If you use a black light (UV torch), a grown-up handles it, and nobody looks into it.

schedule.what: Charge the glow stars with red light and blue light. Compare how they glow in the dark.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the star after red light and after blue light. Draw a few big photons for blue, and many small photons for red.

setup.art: Three glow-in-the-dark star stickers lying on a dark cloth inside a cupboard.
setup.caption: 1. Keep the stars in the dark until they stop glowing.

setup.art: A torch covered with red cellophane shining brightly on one star.
setup.caption: 2. Shine bright red light on one star for 20 seconds.

setup.art: A torch covered with blue cellophane, held further away, shining dimly on another star.
setup.caption: 3. Shine dim blue light on another star for 20 seconds.

setup.art: In the dark, one star glowing green-white and the other star dark.
setup.caption: 4. Switch off. Which star glows?

flow.do: 1. Put 3 glow stars in a dark cupboard for 10 minutes so they stop glowing. 2. Meanwhile, cover the torch with 2 layers of red cellophane. Or set the phone screen to plain red at full brightness.
flow.say: We need the stars to start completely dark. Then any glow comes only from the light we shine on them.
flow.kid: Put the stars in a dark place. Wait until they stop glowing. Get the red light ready.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Glow Star Test. You shine red and blue light on glow-in-the-dark stars to see which colour makes them glow.

flow.do: 1. In the dark room, shine the bright red light on star 1 for 20 seconds, close up. 2. Switch it off. 3. Look at the star.
flow.say: Red light, very bright, very close. Let's see if it charges the star.
flow.kid: Shine the bright red light on star 1. Count to 20. Switch it off. Does it glow?

good: Nothing, or only a very faint glow.

flow.do: 1. Change to blue cellophane, or set the phone screen to plain blue. 2. Hold it further away, so it is dimmer than the red. 3. Shine it on star 2 for 20 seconds. 4. Switch it off and look.
flow.say: This time the light is dimmer, and blue. Let's see what happens.
flow.kid: Now use blue light. Hold it further away, so it is dim. Count to 20. Switch it off. What do you see?

check.q: The bright red light did not make the star glow, but the dim blue light did. Why?
options: Each blue photon carries enough energy, and each red photon does not
check.why: Light comes in packets called photons. A blue photon carries more energy than a red one. To make the star glow, one photon has to give one tiny part of the star a big enough kick. Lots of weak red photons cannot add up to do it. Picking 'too bright' usually means thinking brightness is what matters. Picking 'closer' is a good fair-test thought, but in this test the blue light was further away.

flow.do: Explain what this shows, using the idea of photons.
flow.say: In 1905, Einstein said light comes in packets. Each packet is called a photon. The colour of the light sets how much energy each packet has. Blue packets are strong. Red packets are weaker. A bright red light is just lots of weak packets. It is like trying to knock down a coconut with lots of cotton balls instead of one stone.
flow.kid: Light comes in tiny packets called photons. Blue photons are strong. Red photons are weaker. Many weak ones cannot do what one strong one can.
flow.parent: This is the same idea as the photoelectric effect, which won Einstein his Nobel Prize. There, blue or ultraviolet light knocks electrons out of a metal, but red light cannot, however bright. If you have a UV torch, try it too. It makes the star glow the brightest.

flow.do: Try one more: the bright white torch with no cellophane, on star 3.
flow.say: White light from a torch is a mix of colours. It includes some strong blue photons. Do you think it will charge the star?
flow.kid: Try the white torch on star 3. Does it glow? Why?

ask.q: Why does white light charge the star?
good: White light has blue photons in it.
It has some strong photons mixed in.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like scientists. What do you think? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: blue light can make a glow star glow, but red light cannot. What I saw: the bright red light left star 1 dark, but the dim blue light made star 2 glow. Why: light comes in packets, and each blue packet has enough energy, but each red packet does not.

experiments.title: Chocolate in the Microwave: measure the speed of light
experiments.context: In this experiment, a grown-up melts a plate of chocolate in a microwave oven with the turning plate taken out. The melted spots show the size of the microwaves. From that, you work out their speed. Microwaves are the same kind of wave as light, so they travel at the speed of light.
experiments.question: Can we measure the speed of light in our own kitchen?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the chocolate melt all over evenly? Or will it melt in spots?
experiments.fair_test: Take the turning glass plate out, so the chocolate stays still. Heat it for only a short time, about 15 to 20 seconds, so only the hottest spots melt. Measure between the centres of melted spots, more than once, and take the middle value.

materials.item: a microwave oven, with its turning plate taken out
a flat bar of chocolate, or a few slices of cheese, on a microwave-safe plate
a ruler
a grown-up to run the oven

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up uses the microwave. Never run a microwave empty, and never put metal inside. Heat for 15 to 20 seconds at a time only. Melted chocolate can be very hot, so let it cool before touching.

schedule.what: Melt the chocolate with the turning plate removed. Measure the gap between melted spots. Work out the speed with a grown-up.

experiments.record: Draw the plate of chocolate with its melted spots. Write the gap between two spots. Write the speed you worked out next to the real speed of light.

setup.art: A grown-up lifting the round glass turning plate out of a microwave oven.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up takes out the turning plate.

setup.art: A flat bar of chocolate on a plate in the middle of the empty microwave.
setup.caption: 2. Put the chocolate in. A grown-up heats it for 15 to 20 seconds.

setup.art: A chocolate bar with three shiny melted spots in a row, a ruler measuring the gap between two spots as about 6 centimetres.
setup.caption: 3. Measure the gap between two melted spots.

flow.do: 1. Look at the sticker on the back or side of the microwave. 2. Find the number with 'MHz' after it, usually 2450 MHz.
flow.say: Every microwave has this number on it. It says how many times its waves wiggle each second. 2450 MHz means 2,450 million wiggles every second.
flow.kid: Look for the sticker on the microwave. Find '2450 MHz'. It means its waves wiggle 2,450 million times every second.
flow.context: This is the first step of the microwave chocolate experiment. Microwaves are the same kind of wave as light. By measuring them, you can find the speed of light.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up takes out the turning plate and its ring. 2. Put the chocolate in the middle on a flat microwave-safe plate. 3. Heat for 15 seconds. 4. Take it out and look for melted, shiny spots.
flow.say: The waves inside a microwave make a pattern of hot spots and cold spots. Without the turning plate, the chocolate stays still. So it melts only at the hot spots.
flow.kid: A grown-up heats the chocolate for 15 seconds. Look closely. Can you see shiny melted spots?
flow.parent: If no spots have melted, heat it for 5 more seconds and look again. Don't let the whole bar melt. If your bar is too small, use a plate of cheese slices or a layer of grated chocolate.

flow.do: 1. Find two melted spots next to each other. 2. Measure from the middle of one to the middle of the other. 3. Write it down. 4. Measure another pair, too.
flow.say: The hot spots are half a wave apart. So a whole wave is twice the gap. Let's measure carefully.
flow.kid: Find two melted spots side by side. Measure from middle to middle. Write it down. Do it twice.

check.q: The melted spots are 6 centimetres apart. How long is one whole microwave?
check.why: The hot spots are half a wave apart. So one whole wave is twice the gap, 6 + 6 = 12 centimetres. Picking 6 means taking the gap as a whole wave. Picking 3 means halving instead of doubling.

flow.do: Work out the speed together. A whole wave is about 12 centimetres. It wiggles 2,450 million times a second. Each wiggle moves the wave on by 12 centimetres.
flow.say: Each second, the wave wiggles 2,450 million times. Each wiggle moves it on by 12 centimetres. So in one second it goes 12 times 2,450 million centimetres. That is about 30,000 million centimetres. That is 3 lakh kilometres. The speed of light!
flow.kid: Each wiggle moves the wave 12 centimetres. It wiggles 2,450 million times a second. Multiply them. You get about 3 lakh kilometres a second!
flow.parent: The full sum: 12 cm × 2,450,000,000 = 29,400,000,000 cm per second. That is 294,000 kilometres per second, close to the real 299,792. Your answer may be a little different, because the spots are blurry. Getting within a tenth is excellent for a kitchen.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then share the chocolate.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why does a microwave tell us about light?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. What I think. What I saw. Why. Then eat the chocolate!
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: microwaves travel at about the speed of light. What I saw: the melted spots were about 6 centimetres apart, so the waves were 12 centimetres long. Why: light and microwaves are the same kind of wave, and we multiplied wave size by wiggles each second to get their speed.

activities.title: Switch On the Dark: what do you notice about light?

materials.item: a torch
a dark room, with the curtains closed
a little talcum powder or a dusty cloth

activities.safety: Never shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Explore torchlight in a dark room. Say what you notice and what you wonder.

activities.record: Write or draw one thing you noticed and one thing you wonder about light.
activities.context: This is a short noticing activity to start the unit. In a dark room, you play with a torch and wonder what light is.

setup.art: A child in a dark room switching on a torch pointed at the far wall.
setup.caption: 1. Switch the torch on and off. Watch the far wall.

setup.art: A torch beam made visible as a straight bright line by a puff of talcum powder in the air.
setup.caption: 2. Shake a little powder in the beam. See the straight line.

setup.art: A child's hand trying to grab the torch beam, the light falling on their closed fist.
setup.caption: 3. Try to catch the light in your hand.

flow.do: 1. Close the curtains and switch off the lights. 2. Give your child the torch. 3. Ask them to switch it on and off, pointing at the far wall.
flow.say: Switch the torch on and off. Watch the wall closely. Does the light take any time to get there?
flow.kid: Point the torch at the far wall. Switch it on and off. Does the light take any time to get there?
flow.context: This is the first step of Switch On the Dark. You play with a torch in a dark room and notice how light behaves.

good: The wall lights up the moment I press the switch.

flow.do: 1. Hold the torch steady. 2. Gently shake a little talcum powder, or flap a dusty cloth, in the beam. 3. Look at the beam from the side.
flow.say: Look at the beam from the side. What shape is it? Light only shows up when it bounces off something, like the specks of powder.
flow.kid: Shake a little powder in the beam. Look from the side. What shape is the light?

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to try to catch the light in a closed hand, then open it. 2. Switch off the torch. 3. Ask the big questions below.
flow.say: Can you catch light? Where does the light go when we switch off the torch? What do you think light is made of? There are no wrong answers yet. We'll find out together.
flow.kid: Try to catch the light in your hand. Open your hand. Is it there? Where does the light go when you switch off?

ask.q: What do you wonder about light?

flow.think: When you switch off the torch, does the light stop, or does it fly away somewhere?
flow.parent: This is a noticing step, so don't explain yet. Write down your child's wonders. The rest of the unit will answer many of them. Light does take time to travel, but across a room it is far too fast to notice.

activities.title: The 8-Minute Wait

materials.item: a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand
a long piece of string or wool, about 1 metre
4 clothes pegs or paper clips
a ruler
paper and crayons

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun, not even for a second. It can hurt your eyes for ever.

schedule.what: Feel how long sunlight takes to reach us. Make a small light-time string for the Moon, the Sun and the planets.

activities.record: Write: the sunlight on my arm left the Sun about 8 minutes ago. Draw what you did during the 8-minute wait.
activities.context: This activity helps you feel how long light takes to travel. Sunlight needs about 8 minutes to reach us. You wait 8 minutes and make a string to show light's travel times.

setup.art: A child sitting in a patch of sunlight on the floor, a phone timer showing 8:20 beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Sit in the sunlight. Start an 8 minute 20 second timer.

setup.art: A string laid on the floor with clothes pegs at 0, 8 cm and 43 cm, labelled Sun, Earth and Jupiter.
setup.caption: 2. Lay a string. Every centimetre is one minute of light travel.

setup.art: The child pointing at a tiny peg right next to the Earth peg, labelled Moon, 1 second.
setup.caption: 3. Find the Moon. It is less than a minute from Earth.

flow.do: 1. Find a patch of sunlight indoors, on the floor or a bed. 2. Sit in it with your child. 3. Feel the warmth on your arm.
flow.say: This warm light on your arm has come all the way from the Sun. The Sun is 15 crore kilometres away. Light is the fastest thing there is. Even so, it took about 8 minutes to get here.
flow.kid: Sit in a patch of sunlight. Feel it on your arm. This light came from the Sun. It took about 8 minutes to get here.
flow.context: This is the first step of The 8-Minute Wait. You find out how long sunlight takes to travel from the Sun to you.
flow.parent: Sunlight through a window is safe to sit in. Never let your child look at the Sun itself.

flow.do: 1. Set a timer for 8 minutes and 20 seconds. 2. Start it. 3. While it runs, your child draws the Sun on one side of a page and themselves on the other, with a beam between. 4. When it rings, stop.
flow.say: The light that is landing on you right now left the Sun when we press start. Let's wait for the next lot. That's how long its journey takes.
flow.kid: Start a timer for 8 minutes and 20 seconds. While you wait, draw the Sun, you, and the light between. When it rings, that is how long sunlight takes!

check.q: If the Sun suddenly went dark, when would we find out?
check.why: The last light the Sun gave out would still be on its way. It would take about 8 minutes to reach us. Until then, the sky would stay bright. Picking 'at that very moment' usually means thinking light is instant. Picking 'the next day' mixes it up with night and day, which come from the Earth spinning. The Sun cannot really go dark like this. It has fuel for billions of years.

flow.do: 1. Lay the string straight on the floor. 2. Put a peg at one end. That is the Sun. 3. Measure 8 centimetres along and put the Earth peg there. 4. Put a Mars peg at about 13 centimetres. 5. Put a Jupiter peg at 43 centimetres.
flow.say: Let's make the string a light-clock. Every centimetre is one minute of light travel from the Sun. Earth is 8 minutes away, so it goes at 8 centimetres.
flow.kid: Lay out the string. The Sun is at one end. Every centimetre is one minute of light travel. Put Earth at 8 centimetres. Put Jupiter at 43.
flow.parent: These are average light-times from the Sun. Mars is about 13 light-minutes from the Sun, Jupiter about 43, Saturn about 80. If your string is long enough, Saturn goes at 80 centimetres. The Moon is only about 1 and a third light-seconds from Earth, so its peg sits right on top of the Earth peg.

ask.q: Where would the Moon go on this string?
good: Almost on top of the Earth peg, because it is only about a second away.

flow.do: Talk about how far the nearest star would be on the same string.
flow.say: The nearest star after the Sun is called Proxima Centauri. Its light takes over 4 years to reach us. On our string, where every centimetre is a minute, it would be about 22 kilometres away. That's further than across a whole city!
flow.kid: On this string, the nearest star would be 22 kilometres away. That is across a whole city!
flow.think: When you see a star tonight, how old is the light you are seeing?

activities.title: Ripples in a Thali: what is a wave?

materials.item: a large steel thali or a baking tray
water, about 2 centimetres deep
2 small pebbles or marbles
a torch

activities.safety: Mop up spilt water so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Make ripples in a thali of water. See waves spread, cross and add up. Compare them with rolling marbles.

activities.record: Draw the ripples from one pebble. Then draw the ripples from two pebbles crossing each other.
activities.context: In this activity, you make ripples in a plate of water to see what a wave is. Scientists once argued whether light is a wave like this, or a stream of tiny bits.

setup.art: A steel thali of water on the floor with a torch shining down on it from above.
setup.caption: 1. Fill a thali with a little water. Shine a torch down on it.

setup.art: Rings of ripples spreading from a pebble dropped in the middle of the thali.
setup.caption: 2. Drop one pebble. Watch the rings spread.

setup.art: Two sets of ripple rings crossing each other and making a criss-cross pattern.
setup.caption: 3. Drop two pebbles at once. Watch the ripples cross.

flow.do: 1. Put the thali on the floor and pour in water about 2 centimetres deep. 2. Wait until it is still. 3. Drop one pebble in the middle.
flow.say: Watch the rings spread out. That is a wave. The water itself only bobs up and down. The wiggle is what travels outwards.
flow.kid: Drop one pebble in the middle. Watch the rings spread. That is a wave!
flow.context: This is the first step of Ripples in a Thali. You make water waves to see what a wave is, so you can compare it with light.

ask.q: Does the water travel to the edge, or just the ripple?
good: The water bobs up and down in its place.

flow.do: 1. Hold the two pebbles a hand-width apart above the water. 2. Drop both at the same moment. 3. Shine the torch down onto the water to see the pattern on the bottom of the thali.
flow.say: Where two tops meet, the ripple gets bigger. Where a top meets a dip, they cancel out and the water stays flat. That makes a pattern. Only waves do this.
flow.kid: Drop two pebbles at the same time. Where the ripples cross, look for bigger bumps and flat spots.

check.q: When two ripples cross in the thali, what happens?
options: They add up in some places and cancel out in others
They bounce off each other like balls
The bigger ripple wins and the smaller one stops
check.why: Waves pass through each other. Where two tops meet, they add up. Where a top meets a dip, they cancel. Thomas Young saw the same kind of pattern with light in about 1803, so he said light is a wave. Picking 'bounce' usually means imagining waves as solid things, like balls.

flow.do: Roll two marbles towards each other across a flat floor.
flow.say: Now roll marbles at each other. Do they pass through like ripples? No, they bump. Isaac Newton thought light was made of tiny bits, like very small marbles. Later, scientists found that light does both. It spreads like ripples, and it arrives in tiny packets.
flow.kid: Roll two marbles at each other. They bump! Newton thought light was tiny bits like marbles. Light is both.

ask.q: How are marbles different from ripples?
good: Marbles bump. Ripples pass through each other.
A marble is in one place. A ripple spreads out.

flow.do: Do the founder's wave-and-particle dance: your child moves smoothly like a wave, then in sharp jumps like a particle, when you call out.
flow.say: When I say 'wave', flow your arms like ripples. When I say 'particle', make sharp, tiny jumps, like a photon landing. Light can be both!
flow.kid: Dance! Wave means flowing arms. Particle means sharp little jumps. Light is both.
flow.think: Is light really a wave and really a particle, or are these just our words for it?

activities.title: The Late Moon: act out Rømer's discovery

materials.item: a chair (Jupiter)
a torch (the light from Io)
a ball or a cushion (the Sun)
a messenger: one child or grown-up who walks
a long corridor or a room

activities.safety: Walk, do not run, in a small room.

schedule.what: Act out how Ole Rømer found out light takes time, using a chair for Jupiter and a walking messenger for light.

activities.record: Draw the Sun, the Earth near Jupiter and the Earth far from Jupiter. Write which time Io seemed late.
activities.context: In this acting activity, you show how Ole Rømer, an astronomer in 1676, found out that light takes time to travel. He timed Io, a moon of Jupiter.

setup.art: A chair labelled Jupiter at one end of a corridor, a child holding a torch beside it as Io.
setup.caption: 1. One child is Io beside Jupiter, with a torch.

setup.art: A walking messenger carrying a paper star from Io towards an observer standing close by.
setup.caption: 2. The observer stands near. The messenger walks the news over.

setup.art: The observer standing far down the corridor, the messenger walking a long way with the news.
setup.caption: 3. Now the observer stands far away. The news arrives later.

flow.do: 1. Put the chair at one end of the corridor. It is Jupiter. 2. One child stands by it holding a torch. They are Io, Jupiter's moon. 3. Every time you clap 10 times, Io flashes the torch, to show it coming out of Jupiter's shadow.
flow.say: Io goes round Jupiter like clockwork. Every 42 and a half hours, it comes out of Jupiter's shadow. In our game, it comes out every 10 claps.
flow.kid: You are Io, Jupiter's moon. Every 10 claps, flash the torch. That means you have come out of Jupiter's shadow.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Late Moon. You act out how Ole Rømer found that light takes time to travel.

flow.do: 1. The observer stands 3 steps from Jupiter. 2. Each time Io flashes, the messenger picks up a paper star and walks it to the observer at a slow, steady pace. 3. The observer says 'Now!' when the star arrives.
flow.say: In our game, the light from Io is a slow messenger. Close up, the message arrives quickly after the flash.
flow.kid: Stand close to Jupiter. When Io flashes, the messenger walks the star to you. Say 'Now!' when it arrives.
flow.parent: The messenger stands for light. Walking makes the delay big enough to see. Real light is enormously faster, but Jupiter is enormously far away.

flow.do: 1. The observer moves to the far end of the corridor. 2. Repeat. The messenger walks the same slow pace. 3. Count claps between Io's flash and the observer's 'Now!'.
flow.say: Now the Earth is far from Jupiter. Io flashes on time, but the message takes longer to arrive. So to the observer, Io seems late!
flow.kid: Now stand far away. When Io flashes, wait for the messenger. It takes longer. Io seems late!

check.q: When the Earth was far from Jupiter, Io seemed late. Why?
options: The light carrying the news had further to travel
check.why: Io always came out on time. But the light carrying its picture had a longer trip to reach the Earth. That took extra minutes. Picking 'Io slowed down' is what people first thought. Rømer showed the moon was not late at all. The news was.

flow.do: Tell the real story in a few sentences.
flow.say: In 1676, Ole Rømer worked at the observatory in Paris. He saw that Io seemed later when the Earth was further from Jupiter. He predicted that on 9 November 1676, Io would be about 10 minutes late. It was. He said light needs time to cross space. Many astronomers, even his boss Cassini, did not believe him at first.
flow.kid: In 1676, Ole Rømer saw Io seem late. He said the light was taking time. He predicted Io would be 10 minutes late. It was!

ask.q: Why do you think some astronomers did not believe him?
good: He was young and not famous.
It was a very new idea.

activities.title: Old Starlight Walk: look back in time

materials.item: a clear night and an open place, like a terrace or a field
a torch covered with red cellophane, so your eyes stay used to the dark
a free sky map app on a phone, if you have one
a notebook

activities.safety: A grown-up must come. Stay in a safe, known place. Use a dim red torch so you do not trip.

schedule.what: Go out at night. Find the Moon, a planet and a bright star. Say how old each one's light is.

activities.record: Make a table: the thing I saw, and how long ago its light left it.
activities.context: On this night walk, you look at the Moon, planets and stars. Light takes time to travel, so each one is seen as it was some time ago. You work out how far back in time you are looking.

setup.art: A grown-up and child on a rooftop at night, looking up, the child holding a torch glowing red.
setup.caption: 1. Go out on a clear night. Let your eyes get used to the dark.

setup.art: The night sky with the Moon labelled '1 second ago' and a bright planet labelled 'minutes ago'.
setup.caption: 2. Find the Moon and a bright planet.

setup.art: The constellation Orion with its red star Betelgeuse and bright Sirius below, each labelled with years.
setup.caption: 3. Find a bright star. Its light is years old.

flow.do: 1. Go somewhere dark and safe, away from bright lights. 2. Wait 10 minutes for your eyes to get used to the dark. Use only the red torch. 3. Find the Moon if it is up.
flow.say: Our eyes need time to get used to the dark. While we wait, look at the Moon. Its light left it about one second ago.
flow.kid: Go outside with a grown-up. Wait for your eyes to get used to the dark. Find the Moon. Its light is about one second old.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Old Starlight Walk. You look at the night sky and work out how old the light you see is.
flow.parent: Moonlight is sunlight that bounced off the Moon. So it took 8 minutes to reach the Moon, then about 1 and a third seconds to reach us.

flow.do: 1. Look for a very bright 'star' that does not twinkle much. It is probably a planet, like Venus or Jupiter. 2. Use the sky map app to check its name.
flow.say: Planets shine with sunlight bouncing off them. Their light takes minutes to reach us. Jupiter's light takes between about 33 and 54 minutes.
flow.kid: Find a very bright dot that does not twinkle much. It may be a planet. Its light took minutes to get here.

flow.do: 1. Find a bright star. In winter, look for Orion, the hunter with three stars in a row for his belt. 2. Follow the belt down and left to Sirius, the brightest star. 3. Look at Betelgeuse, the reddish star at Orion's shoulder.
flow.say: Sirius's light left it about 8 and a half years ago. Betelgeuse's light left it about 500 to 700 years ago. Astronomers are still not sure exactly how far it is. When that light set out, there were kings and queens ruling across India who are now in history books.
flow.kid: Find Sirius, the brightest star. Its light left over 8 years ago. Find red Betelgeuse. Its light left hundreds of years ago!

check.q: You see Betelgeuse tonight. Its light left it about 600 years ago. What are you seeing?
options: Betelgeuse as it was about 600 years ago
Betelgeuse exactly as it is tonight
Betelgeuse as it will be in 600 years
check.why: Light from Betelgeuse travelled for hundreds of years to reach you. So you see the star as it was when that light set out. Picking 'as it is tonight' usually means thinking light is instant. Nobody can see the future in a star's light.

flow.parent: At other times of year, find any bright star with the app. It will tell you the star's distance in light-years. That number is also how many years old its light is.

flow.do: At home, fill in the table together.
flow.say: Let's write down how far back in time we looked tonight.
flow.kid: Write each thing you saw. Next to it, write how old its light was.
flow.think: Somewhere far away, someone might be looking at the Sun's light right now. What would they see when they look at us?

activities.title: The Street-Light Star: see light's waves in a cloth

materials.item: a fine cloth with a tight weave, such as an umbrella, a nylon dupatta or a fine tea strainer
a single bright light far away, such as a street light at night

activities.safety: Do it at night only. Never look at the Sun through anything, not even cloth.

schedule.what: Look at a far street light through fine cloth. See a pattern of dots and stripes that only waves can make.

activities.record: Draw the pattern you saw around the street light.
activities.context: In this activity, you look at a faraway light through a fine cloth. A pattern of dots appears around it. This pattern is a clue that light travels as a wave.

setup.art: A child at a window at night holding an umbrella's cloth up to their eye, a street light far away.
setup.caption: 1. At night, hold fine cloth close to your eye.

setup.art: A street light seen through cloth, surrounded by a cross of small bright dots in rows.
setup.caption: 2. Look at a far street light. See the cross of dots.

setup.art: The child turning the cloth, and the cross of dots turning with it.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the cloth. Watch the pattern turn.

flow.do: 1. At night, find a single bright light far away, like a street light. 2. Hold the cloth tight, right up close to one eye. 3. Close the other eye. 4. Look at the light through the cloth.
flow.say: Look closely. Do you see the light as one dot, or as lots of dots in a pattern?
flow.kid: Hold the cloth right up to one eye. Look at a far street light. What do you see?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Street-Light Star. You look at a faraway light through fine cloth to find a clue that light is a wave.

ask.q: What does the light look like?

flow.do: 1. Slowly turn the cloth while you keep looking. 2. Then try a different cloth, or a fine tea strainer.
flow.say: The pattern turns when the cloth turns. The tiny gaps between the threads are making it. When light waves squeeze through tiny gaps, they spread out and cross each other, like the ripples in the thali. Only waves do that.
flow.kid: Turn the cloth slowly. Does the pattern turn too? Try another cloth.

check.q: Why do you see a pattern of dots around the street light?
options: Light waves spread out through the tiny gaps and cross each other
The cloth has tiny lights in it
check.why: The gaps between threads are very tiny. Light waves passing through them spread out and overlap. Where they add up, you see bright dots. This is called diffraction. Picking 'tiny lights in the cloth' means thinking the cloth makes light, but it only lets light through.

flow.do: Talk about what it means.
flow.say: This pattern is a clue that light is a wave. But a phone camera would record the same light as tiny separate hits, the photons. Light is both at once. Scientists still find this strange.
flow.kid: This pattern shows light is a wave. But light also comes in tiny packets. It is both!
flow.think: If light is a wave, what is doing the waving?

activities.title: Draw What Light Is: before and after

materials.item: paper and coloured pencils

schedule.what: Draw what you think light is, before and after this unit, and compare.

activities.record: Keep both drawings. Write one sentence under each: what I thought light was.
activities.context: In this activity, you draw what you think light is. Scientists use drawings like this, called models, to show things too small or fast to see.

setup.art: A child drawing a lamp on the left of a page and an eye on the right, with an empty space between.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a lamp and a wall. Leave space between.

setup.art: The space filled with the child's own idea: wavy lines and small dots travelling from the lamp.
setup.caption: 2. Draw what travels from the lamp to the wall.

setup.art: Two drawings side by side, one marked 'before' and one marked 'after'.
setup.caption: 3. Draw again at the end of the unit. Compare.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to draw a lamp on one side of the page and a wall on the other. 2. Ask them to draw what light looks like on its way, if we could zoom in and slow it down.
flow.say: If we could slow light down and zoom right in, what would we see between the lamp and the wall? Draw your best idea.
flow.kid: Draw a lamp and a wall. What travels from the lamp to the wall? Draw your idea.
flow.context: This is the first step of Draw What Light Is. You draw your idea of what light is, then draw it again at the end of the unit.
flow.parent: Any idea is good. Some children draw lines, some draw dots, some draw nothing. Keep it to compare later.

flow.do: At the end of the unit, ask your child to draw again. Compare the two drawings.
flow.say: Now that you know more, draw it again. What did you add? What did you change?
flow.kid: Draw it again now. What is different?

good: A clock showing it takes time.

check.q: Which drawing best matches what scientists know about light?
options: Tiny packets travelling in straight lines, with a wave pattern
A rope joining the lamp to the wall
check.why: Light travels from the lamp in straight lines. It acts like a wave and arrives in packets called photons. It takes a tiny bit of time. Picking 'nothing, light is instant' was what many people believed before Rømer. Picking 'a rope' means thinking light joins things, but it flies from one to the other.

projects.title: The Cosmic Messenger String

materials.item: a long ball of wool or string, at least 3 metres
12 clothes pegs or paper clips
paper cards and crayons, to make labels
a measuring tape or a ruler
sticky tape

projects.safety: The night sky part needs a grown-up.

schedule.what: Make the string. Peg on the Sun, the planets and their light-minutes.
Go out at night with a grown-up. Find one planet or star from the string.
Add the stars at the end. Present the string to the family as a light-time tour.

projects.record: Take a photo or draw the finished string. Write the light-time of each peg. Write the nearest star's distance on this string.
projects.context: In this 3-day project, you make a long string showing how long light takes to reach each planet from the Sun. Every centimetre is one minute of light travel.

setup.art: A child laying a long string along a corridor floor and pegging a yellow card labelled Sun at one end.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out a long string. Peg the Sun at one end.

setup.art: The string with cards pegged along it: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, spread further apart.
setup.caption: 2. Peg each planet at its light-minutes, 1 centimetre for each minute.

setup.art: The child pointing out of a window, with a sign saying 'nearest star: 22 kilometres down this road'.
setup.caption: 3. Work out where the nearest star would be. It is far beyond the house!

flow.do: 1. Lay out at least 3 metres of string along the floor. 2. Peg the Sun at one end. 3. Measure and peg each planet: Mercury at 3 centimetres, Venus at 6, Earth at 8, Mars at 13, Jupiter at 43, Saturn at 80, Uranus at 160, Neptune at 250.
flow.say: Every centimetre on this string is one minute of light travel from the Sun. The inner planets are crowded close. The outer planets are very far apart.
flow.kid: Peg the Sun at one end. Every centimetre is one light-minute. Earth goes at 8. Neptune goes all the way at 250!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cosmic Messenger String. You make a string where each centimetre is one minute of light travel from the Sun.
flow.parent: These are average light-times from the Sun, rounded: Mercury about 3 minutes, Venus 6, Earth 8, Mars 13, Jupiter 43, Saturn 80, Uranus 160, Neptune 250. Neptune's light-time is over 4 hours.

flow.do: On a clear evening, take your child outside. Use a sky map app to find any planet that is up. Point at it, then find it on the string.
flow.say: Look, that is Jupiter. On our string, it is at 43 centimetres. Its sunlight bounced off it and then travelled to us. That took over half an hour.
flow.kid: Go outside with a grown-up. Find a planet with the app. Which peg on your string is it?
flow.wait: Do this on day 2, on a clear evening.

ask.q: Is the light from Jupiter old or new?
good: A bit old. It took over half an hour to get here.

flow.do: 1. Talk about where the stars would go. 2. Make a card for Proxima Centauri. 3. Work out together how far away it would be on this string. 4. Present the whole string to the family.
flow.say: The nearest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri. Its light takes over 4 years to reach us. On our string, that would be about 22 kilometres away. We couldn't even fit it in our town. The stars are much, much further than the planets.
flow.kid: Make a card for the nearest star. On your string it would be 22 kilometres away! Now give your family a tour of the string.

check.q: On the string, Earth is 8 centimetres from the Sun, and Neptune is 250 centimetres. What does that tell you?
options: Neptune's sunlight takes far longer to arrive than Earth's
Neptune is closer to the Sun than Earth
check.why: Each centimetre is one minute of light travel. So sunlight takes about 250 minutes, over 4 hours, to reach Neptune, but only 8 minutes to reach Earth. Light does not slow down out there. It just has much further to go. Picking 'light slows down' mixes up a longer trip with a slower speed.

flow.parent: Proxima Centauri is about 4.24 light-years away. That is about 22 lakh light-minutes, so about 22 kilometres on a string with 1 centimetre per minute.

challenges.title: Galileo's Lantern Test
challenges.problem: In 1638, Galileo suggested a way to find out if light takes time. Two people stand far apart with lanterns. Can you measure light's speed this way, using torches?
constraints: You may only use two torches, a stopwatch and your helpers.
Stand as far apart as you safely can, at least 50 big steps.
materials: an open space, such as a playground in the evening
general: Galileo's plan: person A uncovers a lantern. As soon as person B sees it, B uncovers theirs. A times how long until they see B's light.
People take about a quarter of a second to react. Light crosses 100 metres in about a three-millionth of a second. So all you are measuring is how fast people react!
To measure light, you need a very long distance, or a very fast clock, or both.
creative: Ole Rømer used the whole width of the Earth's path round the Sun as his distance, and Jupiter's moon as his clock.
Hippolyte Fizeau, in 1849, used a fast-spinning wheel with teeth as his clock. Light went through a gap, off a mirror 8 kilometres away, and was blocked by the next tooth on the way back.
Today, scientists fire laser pulses at mirrors that astronauts left on the Moon in 1969. The light comes back after about 2 and a half seconds.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to show light is not instant. You can use giant distances, clever clocks or the sky. Draw your idea.

setup.art: Two children far apart on a playground at dusk, each holding a torch, one holding a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 1. Stand far apart, each with a torch.

setup.art: Child A switching on a torch, child B far away about to switch theirs on in reply.
setup.caption: 2. A flashes. When B sees it, B flashes back.

setup.art: Child A looking at the stopwatch showing about half a second, with a big thought bubble showing a brain.
setup.caption: 3. Time it. What are you really measuring?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Explain Galileo's plan.
flow.say: Galileo wanted to know if light takes time. He said: I uncover my lantern. You uncover yours as soon as you see mine. I time how long until I see yours.
flow.kid: Galileo had a plan. I flash. You flash back the moment you see mine. I time it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Galileo's Lantern Test. You try Galileo's 1638 plan for measuring the speed of light, using torches.

flow.do: 1. Stand 50 big steps apart. 2. Person A starts the stopwatch and switches on their torch. 3. Person B switches theirs on the moment they see A's. 4. A stops the stopwatch when they see B's light. 5. Repeat 5 times. Then try from just 5 steps apart.
flow.say: Let's try it. Then let's try it from very close. Does the time change?
flow.kid: Try it 5 times from far away. Then try it from close up. Write down each time.
flow.parent: Your times will be about half a second both near and far. That is how long the two people take to react. The light's trip is too tiny to see. Galileo found the same thing.

flow.do: Talk about what you found. Read the general and creative solutions.
flow.say: The time was the same, near or far. So we were not timing the light. We were timing ourselves! Light is far too fast for this test. Rømer used a much longer distance. Fizeau used a much faster clock.
flow.kid: Near or far, the time was the same. We timed ourselves, not the light! Light is too fast for this test.

check.q: In the torch test, the time was about half a second, near or far. What were you really measuring?
check.why: Light crosses 50 steps in far less than a millionth of a second. People take about a quarter of a second to react, each. So the half second is the two people's reaction times. Picking 'the speed of light' is what Galileo hoped, but light was too fast.

flow.do: Ask your child to invent and draw their own way.
flow.say: Now you invent a way. How could you show that light takes time?
flow.kid: Now invent your own way to measure light. Draw it.

challenges.title: Send a Message by Light
challenges.problem: Light is the fastest messenger. Design a way to send a short message, like 'come for dinner', from one room to another, or from one window to another, using only light.
constraints: No talking, no phones and no paper notes.
Your message must work even if the other person cannot hear you.
Test it, and see how fast you can send one word.
materials: paper and pencil to write your code
general: Make a code: one flash for yes, two for no.
Use short and long flashes, like Morse code. Ship crews still use signal lamps like this.
Lighthouses send out their own pattern of flashes, so sailors know which lighthouse they see.
creative: Use coloured cellophane: red, green and blue flashes can mean different things.

In the 1950s, Narinder Singh Kapany, from Punjab, showed that light could be guided along bundles of thin glass threads. Many think he deserved more credit. Today, light flashing billions of times a second in glass fibres under the sea carries the internet between countries.
Long ago, armies sent messages by flashing sunlight off mirrors. This was called a heliograph.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own light code. Teach it to someone in your family and send them a secret message.

setup.art: Two children in rooms facing each other across a courtyard, each with a torch.
setup.caption: 1. Stand where you can see each other but cannot hear.

setup.art: A paper code sheet showing short and long flash marks next to words like 'yes', 'no' and 'dinner'.
setup.caption: 2. Write a light code together.

setup.art: One child flashing a torch in a pattern, the other writing down the flashes and decoding them.
setup.caption: 3. Send a message. Can your partner read it?

flow.do: Make a code sheet together. Give each word or letter its own pattern of short and long flashes.
flow.say: Light is the fastest messenger. People have sent messages with light for thousands of years. Let's invent our own code.
flow.kid: Make a light code. Choose a flash pattern for each word. Try yes, no, come and dinner.
flow.context: This is the first step of Send a Message by Light. You invent a code to send messages with a torch.

flow.do: 1. Go to two places where you can see each other but not hear. 2. Send three messages each way. 3. Time how long each one takes.
flow.say: Send your message. How long does it take? The light itself arrives almost instantly. The slow part is flashing and reading.
flow.kid: Send three messages. Time each one. Was the light slow, or were you?

check.q: Your light message took 20 seconds to send. What took most of the time?
check.why: Light crosses a courtyard in far less than a millionth of a second. All the time went on flashing the code and working it out. That is why fibre-optic cables flash billions of times a second, to send messages faster. Picking 'the light travelling' usually means thinking light is slow over short distances.

flow.do: Read the creative solutions together. Then improve your code.
flow.say: Kapany showed light could be sent along thin glass threads. Today, the internet travels as light flashing in such threads. How could you make your code faster?
flow.kid: Read about glass threads that carry light. Now make your code faster. Try again!

videos.title: Riding a beam of light from the Sun to the Earth, in real time
videos.why: An animation that travels at the real speed of light, so the child can feel how long the 8-minute trip from the Sun takes and how slow it looks across the solar system.

opts: Energy that travels, even through empty space
quiz.why: Light is energy that travels outwards from light sources. It crosses empty space. Picking 'a kind of air' mixes up light with what it shines through.

quiz.p: Which of these needs air to travel, while light does not?
quiz.why: Sound needs air or something else to pass it along. Light and its cousins, like radio waves, cross empty space. Picking 'radio waves' usually means thinking radio is a kind of sound, but it is a kind of light-like wave.

quiz.p: About how fast does light travel in empty space?
opts: No speed at all, it is instant
quiz.why: Light goes about 3 lakh kilometres every second. '1 kilometre in 3 seconds' is the speed of sound. 'Instant' is the old idea that Rømer showed was wrong.

quiz.p: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us. What does that mean when you see the sunrise?
opts: You see the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago
You see the Sun as it will be in 8 minutes
quiz.why: The light took about 8 minutes to travel to you. So you see the Sun as it was when that light left. Picking 'will be' means thinking light shows the future. Picking '8 kilometres' mixes up time and distance.

quiz.p: In the Flash and Bang experiment, which arrived first from 200 steps away?
opts: The flash, the sight of the plates meeting
Both at exactly the same moment
quiz.why: Light is almost a million times faster than sound. From 200 steps, light arrives almost at once and sound a moment later. Picking 'the same moment' is true only when you stand very close.

quiz.p: You count 12 seconds between a lightning flash and its thunder. About how many kilometres away is the lightning?
quiz.why: Sound travels about 1 kilometre every 3 seconds. 12 divided by 3 is 4. So it is about 4 kilometres away.

quiz.p: Ole Rømer found in 1676 that Jupiter's moon Io seemed late when the Earth was far from Jupiter. Why?
opts: The light carrying the news had further to travel
quiz.why: Io was never late. Its light simply had a longer trip. Picking 'Io slowed down' is the first idea most people have, but Rømer showed it was the light that took time.

quiz.p: Galileo's lantern test, with two people on hills, did not show any delay. Why?
opts: Light was far too fast for people to time between two hills
The lanterns were too far apart
quiz.why: Light crosses a few kilometres in a tiny fraction of a second. People react far more slowly. So the test only measured reactions. Picking 'too dim' misses that dim light travels just as fast as bright light.

opts: A single tiny packet of light
quiz.why: Light comes in tiny packets called photons. Picking 'a kind of atom' mixes up photons with the atoms that give them out.

quiz.p: Thomas Young saw bright and dark stripes when light went through two slits. Isaac Newton thought light was tiny bits. Who was right?
opts: Both, in a way: light travels like a wave and arrives in packets
quiz.why: Light makes wave stripes, as Young showed. It also arrives as tiny packets, the photons. Picking only one of them misses that light behaves like both.

quiz.p: In the Glow Star Test, bright red light did not make the star glow, but dim blue light did. What does this show?
opts: Light comes in packets, and each blue packet has more energy than each red one
Blue light is faster than red light
quiz.why: Each blue photon carries enough energy to make the star glow, and each red photon does not. Picking 'blue is faster' is a common mix-up. All colours travel at the same speed in empty space.

opts: The distance light travels in one year
A year that is very bright
The time it takes to make light
quiz.why: A light-year is a distance, about 9 lakh crore kilometres. Picking a time is a very common mix-up, because the word 'year' is in it.

quiz.p: You look at a star 50 light-years away. What are you seeing?
opts: The star as it was about 50 years ago
The star as it is right now
The star as it will be in 50 years
Only a picture painted on the sky
quiz.why: Its light took 50 years to reach you. So you see the star as it was when that light set out. Looking far away is looking back in time.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still NOT know?
opts: What a photon is really like between leaving a lamp and being detected
How long sunlight takes to reach us
Whether light can cross empty space
quiz.why: Light's speed and travel times are measured very exactly, and we know it crosses space. But what a photon really is on its journey is still argued about. That is one of the big open questions in physics.

quiz.p: In quantum physics, an 'observer' must be a person.
quiz.why: False. In physics, an observer is anything that measures, like a detector or a camera. A person does not need to be watching.

applications: The internet travels between countries as flashes of light inside thin glass threads under the sea.
GPS in phones and cars works out where you are from how long radio signals, travelling at the speed of light, take to arrive from satellites.
Scientists measure the Earth to Moon distance to within centimetres by timing laser light bounced off mirrors on the Moon.
ISRO's mission control in Bengaluru talks to spacecraft by radio, and must wait for each message to cross space at the speed of light.
Solar panels on rooftops turn photons from sunlight into electricity.
Phone cameras count photons to make a photo.
Astronomers learn what stars are made of, and how hot they are, from their light.
Telescopes looking at very far galaxies see the young universe, because that light is billions of years old.
Lighthouses and ships' signal lamps send messages by light.
Weather people use the gap between lightning and thunder, and radio signals from lightning, to track storms.
Since 1983, the metre itself is defined by how far light goes in a tiny fraction of a second.
Laser rangefinders on building sites measure distance by timing light.
Gravitational lensing lets astronomers map dark matter, which gives out no light.

open_questions.q: What is a photon really like between leaving a lamp and landing on a detector?
open_questions.why_open: Quantum physics predicts the results perfectly, but scientists disagree about what is actually happening on the way. Several pictures fit the same results.

open_questions.q: Why is the speed of light the number it is, and not some other number?
open_questions.why_open: We have measured it exactly, but nobody knows why the universe has this speed limit and not a different one.

open_questions.q: Is the speed of light the same going one way as coming back?
open_questions.why_open: We can only time light on round trips, there and back. To time a one-way trip, you need two clocks set exactly together, and setting them uses light. Most physicists think it makes no difference, but it cannot be tested directly.

open_questions.q: Can the human eye detect a single photon?
open_questions.why_open: One study in 2016 suggested people sometimes can, but only a few people were tested and the effect was small.

open_questions.q: What is dark matter, which gives out no light at all?
open_questions.why_open: We can see its pull bending light from far galaxies, but nobody has found what it is made of.

open_questions.q: What happened before the oldest light we can see?
open_questions.why_open: The oldest light set out about 380,000 years after the universe began. Before that, the universe was a glowing fog that light could not cross, so we cannot see further back with light.

open_questions.q: Does gravity have its own tiny packets, like light has photons?
open_questions.why_open: Many physicists think gravity might come in packets called gravitons. Nobody has ever detected one, and they may be too weak to ever catch.

open_questions.q: Why does a photon have no mass, and other particles do?
open_questions.why_open: Physics can describe this with sums, but the deeper reason the universe is built this way is still a question.
