maths.problem: In the monsoon, you saw a flash of lightning. You counted 15 seconds until the thunder. Sound goes about 1 kilometre every 3 seconds. How far away was the lightning?
maths.explain: Sound needs 3 seconds for each kilometre. 15 seconds divided into groups of 3 makes 5 groups. 15 ÷ 3 = 5. So the lightning was about 5 kilometres away. Check: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 15.
maths.context: Remember the Flash and Bang experiment? You saw the plates meet before you heard the bang, because light is much faster than sound. Lightning works the same way.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the gap by 3 turns a number of seconds into a distance, so you know if a storm is near.

maths.problem: In the 8-Minute Wait, you set a timer for 8 minutes and 20 seconds, the time sunlight takes to reach us. How many seconds is that altogether?
maths.explain: Each minute has 60 seconds. 8 minutes is 8 × 60 = 480 seconds. Add the 20 extra seconds. 480 + 20 = 500. So sunlight takes about 500 seconds.
maths.context: In the 8-Minute Wait, you sat in sunlight and set a timer for 8 minutes and 20 seconds. That is how long the light took to come from the Sun.
maths.why_maths: Turning minutes into seconds lets us compare the Sun's light-time with the Moon's, which is only about 1 second.

maths.problem: On the Cosmic Messenger String, Earth is at 8 centimetres and Jupiter is at 43 centimetres. Each centimetre is one minute of light travel from the Sun. How many more minutes does sunlight take to reach Jupiter than to reach Earth?
maths.explain: 43 − 8 = 35. So sunlight takes about 35 minutes longer to reach Jupiter. Check: 8 + 35 = 43.
maths.context: In the Cosmic Messenger String project, you pegged each planet on a string. Each centimetre stood for one minute of light travel from the Sun.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting tells us how much further Jupiter is, in light-minutes. That gap is what made Rømer's moon seem late.

maths.problem: Light can go round the Earth about 7 and a half times in one second. How many times could it go round in 2 seconds? In 4 seconds?
maths.answer: 15 times in 2 seconds, and 30 times in 4 seconds.
maths.explain: In 1 second, 7 and a half times. In 2 seconds, double that: 7 and a half + 7 and a half = 15. In 4 seconds, double again: 15 + 15 = 30.
maths.context: This is about how fast light is. It can travel round the whole Earth about seven and a half times in one second.
maths.why_maths: Doubling shows how quickly light's distances pile up, even in a few seconds.

maths.problem: In the Chocolate experiment, the melted spots were 6 centimetres apart. The spots are half a wave apart. How long is one whole wave? If the spots were 5 centimetres apart, how long would the wave be?
maths.answer: 12 centimetres. And 10 centimetres for spots 5 centimetres apart.
maths.explain: A whole wave is two halves. 6 + 6 = 12 centimetres. For spots 5 centimetres apart, 5 + 5 = 10 centimetres.
maths.context: In the microwave chocolate experiment, a grown-up melted chocolate with the turning plate taken out. It melted in spots, because of the waves inside.
maths.why_maths: Measuring the spots in centimetres, then doubling, gives the size of the wave. With the wiggles per second, that gives the speed of light.

maths.problem: In the Flash and Bang experiment, you stood 100 big steps away and then 200 big steps away. Sound takes about 1 second for every 500 big steps. Roughly how long did the bang take from 200 big steps? Is it more or less than half a second?
maths.answer: About 2 fifths of a second, which is less than half a second.
maths.explain: 500 big steps take about 1 second. 200 big steps is less than half of 500, because half of 500 is 250. So the bang took less than half a second. The flash took almost no time at all.
maths.context: In the Flash and Bang experiment, a helper banged steel plates far away. You saw them meet before you heard the bang.
maths.why_maths: Comparing with a half helps us see how small but real the sound's delay is, and how tiny light's is.

roots.context: We have been learning what light is and how fast it travels. Now we ask what light tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Everything you see is a message from the past. There is no single 'now' that you can see.
deep_truth.habit: We think of 'now' and 'then' as clean, separate boxes, and we think seeing is instant. But every sight arrives a little late. The Sun is 8 minutes ago, a star is years ago, your friend's face a tiny moment ago. The world you see is made of many 'thens' arriving together.
deep_truth.evidence: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us. Rømer's moon Io seemed late because its light needed extra time to cross space.

three.who_am_i: You are made of atoms forged in stars, and you are fed by sunlight caught in plants. In a real way, you are made of old light.
three.what_is_life: Life runs on light. Plants catch photons from the Sun, and every living thing that eats depends on them.
three.what_is_this_world: The sky is a huge bundle of old letters, all arriving at once. Light ties every corner of the universe to every other.

roots.thread: Light is one thing that shows up in many ways. It is a wave and a packet, a warmth and a picture, a radio signal and a rainbow, all one kind of wiggle. It leaves a star and travels for years, then becomes part of what you see, and what a plant makes into food. DeepKids believes this is the One becoming the many: one light, everywhere at once, carrying news from every part of the universe to every other. When you see a star, the star and you are joined by the light between you.

teachings.teaching: King Janaka asks the sage Yajnavalkya: what light does a person live by? The Sun, says the sage. And when the Sun has set? The Moon. And when the Moon has set? Fire. And when the fire goes out? Speech. And when speech is silent? Then the self is his light.
teachings.link: We learn that every outside light is a messenger, and all of it arrives a little late. The sage asks about the light that knows all these lights. Is it outside us, or inside?

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, the Buddha's story of the blind men and the elephant (also told in Jain teaching on anekantavada, many-sidedness)
teachings.teaching: Some blind men each touch one part of an elephant. One feels the trunk and says it is a snake. One feels a leg and says it is a pillar. Each is partly right, and they quarrel.
teachings.link: Young's slits said light is a wave. Einstein's packets said it is a particle. Each experiment touched one side of light. Light is bigger than either word.

teachings.teaching: The face of truth is hidden by a golden disc. Uncover it, so that I may see what is true.
teachings.link: The bright Sun dazzles us. But what we see is its old light, a covering, not the Sun as it is now. To see truly, we must look past the shining surface.

science.text: Light from far away is old. Looking further away really is looking further back in time.

In quantum physics, light behaves like a wave and arrives as packets. What a photon is really like between leaving and arriving is still argued about. Here 'observer' means any measuring machine, not a mind. Quantum physics does not prove that consciousness makes the world.

other_view.who: Many physicists, and the old Indian Charvaka school
other_view.view: Light is simply an electromagnetic field doing what the equations say. Calling it a messenger or a sign of oneness is a pretty picture, not science. They think there is no need for any One behind it, and that is an honest view.

practice.title: The Old Light Breath
practice.say: Sit near a window or in a patch of daylight. Close your eyes and feel the light warming your face. Breathe in slowly while I count to four. Breathe out while I count to four. This warmth left the Sun about 8 minutes ago. Its energy may have wandered inside the Sun for thousands of years before that. Now it is resting on you. Breathe in once more. Open your eyes slowly and look at the light in the room. Is it old, or new?
practice.kid: Sit in the daylight. Close your eyes. Feel the light on your face. Breathe in for four. Breathe out for four. This light left the Sun 8 minutes ago. Open your eyes slowly.
